mem.t: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.

lessons.title: We Are God's Workmanship
lessons.theme: My worth lies not in what I do, but in whose handiwork I am

v: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.
For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb.
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.

lessons.still: Rest your hands open on your knees, like a piece of work cradled in a craftsman's hands. Breathe in slowly, breathe out, and say to the Lord, “Lord, I am made by your own hand.” Let the voices that compare and belittle grow quiet, one by one.
teach: In the hands of an amateur, a piece of uncut jade is just a rough stone; in the hands of a master carver, it becomes a family heirloom. Its worth lies not in the stone itself but in the hands that shape it. In the first stage we came home and saw the self-ruled life for what it is. In this second stage we are to put down deeper roots, and the first step is to rediscover whose handiwork I am.

The word translated “workmanship” carries the sense of “something carefully crafted”; some versions render it “masterpiece.” In verse 1 Paul says we were “dead in transgressions and sins,” yet in verse 10 he says we were “created in Christ Jesus.” The dead cannot create themselves; it is God who creates us anew in Christ. Even the good works we are to do are ones God “prepared before.”

People living the self-ruled life try to prove themselves through performance, achievement and the approval of others, so it is never enough and they are never at rest. People living the self-emptied life receive their identity from God's hand, so they have nothing left to prove. Here is the change of mindset: from “I do well, therefore I have worth” to “I am God's workmanship, therefore I walk in the good works he has prepared.” Identity comes first; behaviour follows.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-ruled life wants to carve itself, to be lord of its own life; the self-emptied life hands itself back to the Craftsman — letting people be people and letting God be God. Our identity comes from God, and the good works were prepared by God too, so all the glory goes to Jesus, not to the workmanship.
q: Who is God? — How does it feel to know God shaped you with his own hands and prepared good works for you?
Who am I? — What do you most often use to prove your worth — grades, income, other people's approval?
How shall I respond? — What small good work “God prepared” are you willing to walk in today?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was baptised, before he had performed a single miracle, he heard the Father say, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” His ministry flowed from his identity; it was not a way of earning one. In him, we too are first accepted, and then we go out to do good.
lessons.pray: God my Creator, thank you for making me new in Christ. I will no longer prove myself by performance and comparison; I receive the identity you give me. Open my eyes today to the good works you have prepared, and make me glad to walk in them, so that the glory goes to you and not to me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down three things you often use to prove yourself, and hand each one over to the Lord
When you look in the mirror, say: “I am God's workmanship, made by his own hand.”
Watch for one small good work God has prepared for you, and do it
lessons.noon: “For we are his workmanship” — Lord, right now I place myself back in your hands.

lessons.title: Beloved Children
lessons.theme: God has not only forgiven me; he has adopted me as his child

v: See how great a love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God! For this cause the world doesn’t know us, because it didn’t know him.
For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”
The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God;

lessons.still: Sit quietly, like a child sitting beside their father — no need to perform, no need to speak. Softly call out, “Abba, Father.” Repeat it a few times, and let the name drop slowly from your lips into your heart.
teach: A pardoned prisoner walks out of jail free to start over, yet may still have no home to go to. An adopted child is not only released from the past but given a name, a home and a father. The gospel is not only pardon; it is adoption. In the first week we saw the prodigal come home; today we see what standing the one who has come home has in the house.

John marvels, “how great a love the Father has given to us,” and the Greek adds, “and we are!” — not a figure of speech, but a fact. Paul contrasts two spirits: the spirit of bondage “again to fear,” always worried that failure will get us thrown out, and the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!” “Abba” is a child's most intimate word for a father, and the Holy Spirit himself testifies in our hearts to this identity.

Many Christians are saved, yet still serve with the heart of a slave: afraid of failing, afraid of punishment, straining to perform. Such people tire easily and judge others easily. Here is the change of mindset: I read the Bible and pray not to hold on to my status, but because I am a child who loves being with the Father. A child obeys out of love; a slave obeys out of fear.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The slave's heart is still self-centred — fixed on my performance, my security; the child's heart is fixed on the Father. Live from the heart by the Spirit, and the Spirit bears witness within you; live from the head by yourself, and you fall into calculation and unrest. Live from the heart and you find joy; live from the head and you find worry.
q: Who is God? — “How great a love” — how would you describe the Father who calls you his child?
Who am I? — Is your service more like a child's, or like a hired hand who fears being dismissed?
How shall I respond? — At what moment today will you come before God with an “Abba, Father” heart?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane, deeply distressed, Jesus still prayed, “Abba, Father.” In his darkest hour he still trusted the Father as a Son. He came precisely to share that name with us, making us fellow heirs with him.
lessons.pray: Abba, Father, thank you not only for forgiving me but for adopting me as your child. I lay down the fearful heart of a slave and stop trying to keep your love by performing. Holy Spirit, bear witness in my heart, so that today I draw near to you and obey you with a child's joy and trust. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Begin your prayers today by quietly calling “Abba, Father” three times
Write down one thing you do out of fear of punishment, and start doing it out of love instead
Give a child or younger person a word of affirmation with no strings attached
lessons.noon: “See how great a love the Father has given to us” — Lord, right now I rest in your arms like a child.

lessons.title: A Royal Priesthood
lessons.theme: Being chosen is not a privilege to flaunt but a call to serve

v: But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light.
In the past, you were not a people, but now are God’s people, who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.

lessons.still: Picture yourself standing between God and someone you care about. First turn quietly toward God and receive his presence; then turn toward that person and gently bring their name before God. This is the place of a priest.
teach: A bridge is valuable because it joins two banks. A bridge that cared only about looking good and let no one cross would have lost its reason to exist. Peter says we are “a royal priesthood” — and a priest is exactly that: a bridge, with one end toward God and the other toward people.

Peter uses four titles: a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession. These were originally God's names for Israel in the Old Testament (Exodus 19:6); now they belong to those who are in Christ. The purpose is to “proclaim the excellence” of God. Verse 10 reminds us that we once were “not a people” and “had not obtained mercy” — this identity is grace from start to finish, leaving no room to boast.

Putting “royal” and “priesthood” together is a cure for the self-ruled life. Royal does not mean ruling over others; it means belonging to the true King. Priest does not mean being above others; it means praying for people and serving them. Here is the change of mindset: my identity is not for being served, but for bringing people to God. People matter more than tasks, and everyone I meet is my harvest field.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Only when we let Jesus reign do we have true royalty; only when we let Jesus receive all the glory are we true priests — proclaiming his excellence, not ours. The “2” in 920 are the people God has entrusted to me as a priest: I pray for them and live the self-emptied life before them.
q: Who is God? — How has the God who called you “out of darkness into his marvelous light” brought you out of darkness?
Who am I? — Do you treat being chosen as a mark of superiority, or as a responsibility?
How shall I respond? — Which of your “2” will you stand before God for in prayer today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is our great High Priest. On the night he was betrayed, he prayed for his disciples and also for “those who will believe in me through their word” (John 17). He offered not only prayers but himself; and today he always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25).
lessons.pray: Lord, I was once not a people, but you had mercy on me and called me out of darkness into your marvelous light. Make me a bridge that carries your love to people and brings people to you. May what I proclaim be your excellence, not my own. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: List three of your “2” and pray for each of them for one minute today
Briefly share with a friend how God brought you out of darkness
As you serve today, remind yourself: “I am a bridge, not a stage.”
lessons.noon: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” — Lord, right now make me your bridge.

lessons.title: The Body of Christ
lessons.theme: I am not an island but a member of a body

v: For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ.
When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. When one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.
Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.

lessons.still: Notice how your hands, feet and breathing all work together; no part acts alone. Thank the Lord for placing you in his body. Quietly bring to mind the faces of two or three brothers and sisters, and say thank you to God for them.
teach: However nimble a finger is, cut off from the hand it cannot play the piano. However hot a coal is, lift it out of the fire and it soon goes cold. Christian identity was never meant to be solitary. The first three lessons spoke of “me” as God's workmanship, child and priest; today we say that this “me” lives within an “us.”

Paul says, “the body is one, and has many members” — unity is not uniformity, and diversity is not division. Verse 26 says that when one member suffers, the whole body suffers; when one is honoured, the whole body rejoices. The “you” in verse 27 is plural: the church is not a place I go to but a body I belong to. The head is Christ — not me, and not any leader.

The self-ruled life shows up in church in two ways: the proud say, “I have no need of you,” and the insecure say, “Because I'm not the hand, I'm not part of the body” (12:15, 21). Both are focused on self. Those living the self-emptied life see that I need others and others need me. Relationships matter more than things: life first, then relationships, then ministry. When the body is healthy, ministry naturally bears fruit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: To build what belongs to God is to let Christ be the head while every member works together in love. The spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, and fellow soldiers of 235 are the joints that bind the body together. Pride stirs up pride and the body is wounded; humility draws out humility and every member wins.
q: Who is God? — How does Christ, the head, regard the weakest member of his body?
Who am I? — Are you more likely to say “I have no need of you,” or “I'm not part of the body”?
How shall I respond? — How will you weep with a member who is suffering, or rejoice with one who is honoured?
lessons.jesus: When Saul was persecuting the church, the risen Jesus said to him, “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). The Lord took the church's suffering as his own. He loves the church and gave himself up for her; the church is his body on earth.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the head of the church, and I am a member of your body. Tear down the pride in me that says “I have no need of you,” and heal the insecurity that says “I don't matter.” Teach me to weep and rejoice with my brothers and sisters and to work together in love, so that you receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Send a greeting to a brother or sister who hasn't been around lately
Pray for a member who is suffering, and let them know you did
Say a word of appreciation to a co-worker whose gifts differ from yours
lessons.noon: “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.” — Lord, right now join me to your body.

lessons.title: Living Out Our Identity in God
lessons.theme: Walking worthy of our calling — turning identity into daily life

v: I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called,
with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love,
being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;

lessons.still: Recall this week's four identities: God's workmanship, a beloved child, a royal priest, a member of Christ's body. With each one, take a deep breath and say “thank you” to the Lord. Then ask, “Lord, how shall I live this out today?”
teach: Imagine a prince who grows up lost among the common people. If he never learns who he is, he will go on living like a beggar; but once he knows, the way he speaks and carries himself gradually changes. This week we have rediscovered our identity: God's workmanship, a beloved child, a royal priest, the body of Christ. Today we turn that identity into daily life.

The first three chapters of Ephesians describe what God has done for us; only in chapter 4 does Paul tell us how to walk. His order is always grace first, then response. To walk “worthily of the calling,” the very first thing is “humility,” followed by gentleness, patience, bearing with one another and keeping unity. Colossians is the same: “as God's chosen ones,” therefore “put on” compassion and kindness. Who we are comes first; how we live follows.

Change your mindset and you change your life; change your life and you change your lifestyle, and then your relationships and ministry. Identity is not a slogan to memorise but a choice made in every reaction. When I am misunderstood, I am a beloved child and need not rush to defend myself; when conflict comes, I am a member of the body and work hard to keep unity. Next week we will study Philippians and see how Paul lived out this identity in chains.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Moving from “what I must become” to “what I already am” is a change of perspective — from the human view to God's view. Humility and gentleness, bearing with one another: this is the pattern of the self-emptied life. Self-rule fights for position; self-emptying guards unity. A life like this is building what belongs to God.
q: Who is God? — How does the God who gives grace first and calls second shape the way you see your own weakness?
Who am I? — Of this week's four identities, which moved you most? Which do you find hardest to believe?
How shall I respond? — In which relationship today will you “walk worthily of the calling”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus, “knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came from God, and was going to God,” got up and washed his disciples' feet (John 13:3–5). The clearer our identity, the more freely we can stoop to serve.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for showing me who I am: your workmanship, your child, your priest, a member of your body. Make my words and reactions today worthy of the grace you have given. Give me humility and gentleness in conflict and steadiness when I am misunderstood, so that you receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write this week's four identities on a card and carry it with you
In a conversation that could turn into conflict, choose to answer gently first
Memorise this week's verse: Ephesians 2:10
lessons.noon: “Beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called” — Lord, right now let me live out the identity you have given me.

mem.t: I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.

lessons.title: A Book of Joy Written in Prison
lessons.theme: In chains, Paul wrote a letter brimming with joy

v: I thank my God whenever I remember you,
always in every request of mine on behalf of you all, making my requests with joy,
for your partnership in furtherance of the Good News from the first day until now;
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.

lessons.still: Imagine yourself sitting beside Paul — a bare prison cell, yet filled with thanksgiving. Be still for a moment, and bring before the Lord whatever situation makes you feel “trapped” right now. Say, “Lord, you are here, so I can rejoice.”
teach: Some flowers bloom only at night; the darkness actually brings out their fragrance. Philippians is that kind of letter. Paul wrote it in chains, his future uncertain, yet “joy” appears again and again. This week we will work slowly through the book using the four Bible-reading steps we learned in the first stage: Read, Reflect, Pray, Do.

The church at Philippi was the first church Paul planted in Europe (Acts 16). Its first members included Lydia, the seller of purple cloth; a slave girl set free from a spirit; and the jailer who came to faith after hearing Paul and Silas singing hymns at midnight. Whenever Paul remembered them he gave thanks, because of their “partnership in furtherance of the Good News,” and he was confident God “will complete it.” The key sentence of the whole book is: “For to me to live is Christ.”

Paul's joy did not depend on his circumstances but on a single focus: Christ. In chapter 1 he says his chains have actually advanced the gospel (1:12), and even when some preach Christ out of envy, he rejoices (1:18). Those focused on themselves feel wronged at every turn; those focused on Christ see God at work at every turn. This week, let us ask the Lord to bring our focus back into line as well.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Focus on Jesus — not on yourself, not on others, not on your circumstances. Paul lived this out in prison. “To live is Christ” is the self-emptied life itself: it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. The self-emptied life is not loss; it is entry into the limitless.
q: Who is God? — The God who “will complete it” — what unfinished work is he doing in you right now?
Who am I? — Right now, is the focus of your life Christ, yourself, other people, or your circumstances?
How shall I respond? — Like Paul, how can you find reasons for thanksgiving in today's “chains”?
lessons.jesus: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus told his disciples he wanted his joy to remain in them (John 15:11). The cross was right before him, yet his joy was not taken away, because his focus was on the Father's will. Paul's joy came from this very Lord.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that he who began a good work in me will complete it. Turn my focus away from my circumstances and away from myself, back to you. May I too be able to say, “For to me to live is Christ,” and give thanks for your work even in hard places. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: This week, read through the four chapters of Philippians over four days, using Read, Reflect, Pray, Do
Write down something that makes you feel trapped, and next to it write one thing you are thankful for
Thank God for a partner who shares with you in furthering the gospel — and tell them
lessons.noon: “For to me to live is Christ.” — Lord, right now I turn my focus back to you.

lessons.title: Having the Mind of Christ
lessons.theme: The secret of unity is counting others better than yourself

v: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name,
that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth,
and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

lessons.still: Quietly bring to mind someone who has recently made you uncomfortable. Don't rush to sort out who was right; simply place them before the Lord and say, “Lord, put your mind in me, so that I count them better than myself.”
teach: Two goats meet on a narrow log bridge. If both insist on crossing first, they both fall into the river; if one lies down and lets the other step over, both reach the far bank safely. Pride stirs up pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. The church at Philippi had its quarrels too (4:2), and Paul's remedy was the mind of Christ.

In the first week we read 2:5–8 and saw Christ emptying himself. Today we look at what comes before and after. Before it are commands: no rivalry, no conceit, “each counting others better than himself.” After it comes the outcome: God “highly exalted him,” and every knee will bow to him. Christ's descent was not defeat but the road to glory — and that road is our road too.

“Counting others better than himself” does not mean pretending to think little of yourself; it means choosing to put others' needs first, looking “also to the things of others.” The self-ruled heart asks, “What do I get?” The mind of Christ asks, “What can I give?” Here is the change of mindset: unity does not depend on everyone agreeing, but on each person being willing to bow low first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to our place. Christ emptied himself, and God highly exalted him; when we let Jesus reign, we no longer need to grab for empty glory. This passage ends “to the glory of God the Father” — letting Jesus receive all the glory is our end point too.
q: Who is God? — God exalted the Christ who humbled himself. What does that show you about God?
Who am I? — In which relationship are you competing for “conceit,” for empty glory?
How shall I respond? — How can you concretely look “to the things of others” today?
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper the disciples were still arguing over who was greatest, yet Jesus said, “I am in the middle of you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). He did not crush their pride with authority; he healed it with his own humility.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you willingly humbled yourself. Put your mind in me, so that I stop chasing empty glory and gladly count others better than myself. Wherever I am contending with others, teach me to bow low first, so that God the Father is glorified. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: In a discussion, ask for the other person's view before giving your own
Bless, in a concrete way, someone you have been quietly comparing yourself with
Do one thing that looks “to the things of others,” expecting nothing in return
lessons.noon: “But in humility, each counting others better than himself” — Lord, right now let me bow low first.

lessons.title: Forgetting What Is Behind, Straining Toward What Is Ahead
lessons.theme: Treasuring the knowledge of Christ above all, and pressing on toward the goal

v: However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.

Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ
Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Open your hands and imagine them holding your past achievements and your past hurts. Lay them down one by one, telling the Lord, “I give all of these to you.” Then, with empty hands, lift your head and look ahead to the Lord.
teach: A runner who keeps looking back will either stumble or fall behind; a runner clutching a trophy can't run fast. In chapter 3 Paul lists the credentials he once took pride in — his pedigree, his righteousness under the law, his religious zeal — and then says he considers all of it “a loss.”

Paul uses a merchant's bookkeeping language: “gain” and “loss.” The credentials once listed in the income column are all moved to the loss column, even counted as “refuse,” because he has found the supreme treasure: the knowledge of Christ Jesus his Lord. “Forgetting the things which are behind” is not amnesia; it means no longer letting past successes or failures define us. “Stretching forward” means running hard toward God's upward call.

The self-ruled life often lives in the past. Living in past glory, we grow proud; living in past hurts, we grow bitter; living in past failures, we sink into self-pity. All three are focused on self. Here is the change of mindset: my worth is not in my past but in Christ; my direction is not behind me but in God's upward call.
lessons.light: 321 Light: This is a change of perspective — from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal. Paul exchanged “a righteousness of my own” for the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ (3:9). This is the self-emptied life: laying down our own capital and gaining the riches of Christ. The self-emptied life is not having nothing; it is treasuring Christ above all.
q: Who is God? — Knowing Christ was worth so much that Paul counted everything else as loss. Have you experienced how precious he is?
Who am I? — What do you most often look back on — past glory, past hurts, or past failures?
How shall I respond? — What one thing “behind” will you lay down today so you can run forward?
lessons.jesus: Jesus, “for the joy that was set before him, endured the cross, despising its shame” (Hebrews 12:2). His eyes were fixed on the Father's will and the glory to come. As we run our race, we too look to Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are my greatest treasure. I give you my past achievements, and I give you my past hurts and failures too. Free me from being bound by what lies behind, and help me run single-mindedly toward your call. Knowing you is my supreme treasure. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Draw a line: on the left write “counted as loss,” on the right write “supreme treasure”
Today, when an old wound comes to mind, turn your thoughts and say, “I am running forward.”
Write down one direction in which God is calling you upward this year
lessons.noon: “Forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before” — Lord, right now I run toward you.

lessons.title: Rejoice in the Lord Always
lessons.theme: Joy is not a mood but a choice we make in the Lord

v: Rejoice in the Lord always! Again I will say, “Rejoice!”
Let your gentleness be known to all men. The Lord is at hand.
In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Name the worries in your heart one by one, and after each one add, “Thank you, Lord.” When you have finished, be still for a minute, and let the peace of God that surpasses all understanding stand like a guard at the door of your heart.
teach: A thermometer only reflects the temperature around it; a thermostat changes the temperature of the room. Many people's joy is like a thermometer — up when things are good, down when things are bad. Paul wants us to be thermostats: “Rejoice in the Lord always.” Notice: “in the Lord” — not in our circumstances, and not in ourselves.

This passage has a clear order: joy (toward God) → gentleness (toward others) → not being anxious (toward ourselves) → prayer, petition and thanksgiving (entrusting) → peace (God's response). “Guard” is originally a military word for a garrison holding a city. When we hand over our worries, God's peace stands guard over our hearts and thoughts in Christ Jesus.

“In nothing be anxious” does not tell us to be irresponsible; it tells us not to let worry sit in the master's seat. Worry is actually a hidden form of the self-ruled life: I want to control the outcome myself. Thanksgiving, by contrast, acknowledges that God is in charge. Live from the heart by the Spirit and you have peace; live from the head by yourself and worry grows.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart and you find joy; live from the head and you find worry. Turning worry into prayer is laying down power and letting God be God; adding thanksgiving lets Jesus receive the glory. Those who give thanks in everything find that their joy no longer rises and falls with their circumstances.
q: Who is God? — “The Lord is at hand.” How does this change the way you see your difficulties?
Who am I? — Is your joy more like a thermometer or a thermostat?
How shall I respond? — Which worry will you hand to God today with “prayer + thanksgiving”?
lessons.jesus: As the storm raged and the disciples panicked, Jesus was asleep in the stern on a cushion (Mark 4:38). His peace did not come from the absence of storms but from complete trust in the Father. This Lord lives in us, and his peace becomes the guard at the door of our hearts.
lessons.pray: Lord, I hand you the worries in my heart one by one. Thank you that you are in control of everything and that you are near. Guard my heart and my thoughts with your peace that surpasses all understanding, so that today I rejoice in you always and treat others with gentleness. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Turn one worry into a written prayer, and add a line of thanks
Today, whenever a complaint is about to come out, first say, “Thank you, Lord”
With a gentle heart, let someone else go first in some small matter
lessons.noon: “Rejoice in the Lord always!” — Lord, right now I choose to rejoice in you.

lessons.title: The Secret of Doing All Things
lessons.theme: The secret of contentment lies not in our circumstances but in the Lord who strengthens us

v: Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it.
I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In any and all circumstances I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need.
I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.
My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Quietly count what you have right now, and also admit what you lack. Place both in the Lord's hands and say, “Lord, plenty and want are both in your hands; leaning on you is enough for me.”
teach: Philippians 4:13 is often printed on sports jerseys, as if it meant, “If I just have enough faith, I'll win the game.” But read the context and you find that the “all things” Paul means are being humbled and abounding, being hungry and being filled. This is not a slogan for success; it is the secret of contentment.

Paul says contentment is something he has “learned”; it did not come naturally. The word “secret” originally referred to being initiated into a mystery. Between plenty and hunger he learned that strength lies not in circumstances but in “him who strengthens me.” Verse 19 says God will supply “according to his riches in glory” — not according to our desires, but according to his riches and his good purpose.

The self-ruled life measures God by circumstances: in good times, God is good; in hard times, God is absent. Those living the self-emptied life lean on the Lord in every situation — not proud in plenty, not complaining in want. This week in Philippians we have seen that joy, humility, pressing on and contentment all flow from “to live is Christ.” Next week we will learn confession and forgiveness through prayer, so that this life can put down even deeper roots.
lessons.light: 321 Light: “Through Christ” is the centre of the whole verse — not “I can,” but “through him.” The self-ruled life says, “I can”; the self-emptied life says, “The Lord can, and through him I can.” This is the self-emptied life overcoming the self-ruled life. The glory goes not to a capable me but to the Lord who gives strength.
q: Who is God? — How has the God who supplies according to his riches in glory provided for you in a time of need?
Who am I? — In which situation — plenty or want — do you find it hardest to be content?
How shall I respond? — In what matter today will you say, “Through the Lord, I can”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20), yet he never lacked the Father's presence. He said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). His contentment flowed from his relationship with the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord who gives me strength, I confess that on my own I can do nothing. Thank you for being with me in plenty and in want. Teach me the secret of contentment — not proud in plenty, not complaining in want — leaning on you in everything and giving the glory to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down one thanksgiving from a time of plenty and one from a time of want
Memorise this week's verse: Philippians 4:13
Share with a spiritual companion the verse from Philippians that touched you most this week
lessons.noon: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.” — Lord, right now I lean on you.

mem.t: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

lessons.title: Confession: Taking God's Side
lessons.theme: Confession is not putting ourselves down but standing on God's side

v: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.

lessons.still: Quietly ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: “Lord, show me what I need to confess today.” Don't rush to explain, and don't rush to blame yourself; simply draw back the curtains and let the light come in.
teach: If a patient tells the doctor, “There's nothing wrong with me,” even the best doctor cannot help. John puts it bluntly: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” In the first stage we saw that the self-ruled life is the root problem; this week we learn how to deal with it honestly in our daily prayers.

The word “confess” literally means “to say the same thing.” To confess sin is to say about sin what God says about it — to stand on God's side. It is not a vague “I'm not good,” but a specific “This is sin.” God forgives because he is “faithful” (he keeps his covenant) and “righteous” (Christ has paid sin's price in full) — not because our confession is anguished enough, but because the work of the cross is finished.

The self-ruled life responds to sin in one of two ways: covering it up (shifting blame, rationalising), or punishing itself (as if enough self-reproach could pay for it). Either way, self is handling the sin. Proverbs says, “He who conceals his sins doesn't prosper.” Here is the change of mindset: confession does not lower our standing; it is a child coming back to the Father. The sooner we confess, the sooner we are free.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Confession is humility at its most concrete: laying down the power to defend ourselves, returning to our place as creatures, and letting God be the God who judges and the God who forgives. Pride says, “It's not my fault”; humility says, “I was wrong” — and that is where revival begins.
q: Who is God? — How can a God who is both “faithful” and “righteous” forgive without compromising his justice?
Who am I? — When you face your own sin, do you lean toward covering it up or punishing yourself?
How shall I respond? — What one thing today do you need to name specifically and say, “This is sin”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus had no sin, yet at the Jordan he was baptised alongside sinners (Matthew 3:13–15), standing among them. On the cross he bore our sin, so when we confess, we face not a cold judge but a Saviour who shed his blood for us.
lessons.pray: Faithful and righteous God, I will no longer say I have no sin, and I will no longer defend myself. I confess that … is sin, and that I have sinned against you. Thank you for forgiving me through the precious blood of Jesus and cleansing me from all unrighteousness. Help me to walk in the light every day. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Before bed, spend three minutes reviewing the day and confess one specific thing
Once, replace “I wasn't wrong, it's just that…” with “I was wrong”
Memorise this week's verse: 1 John 1:9
lessons.noon: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous.” — Lord, right now I stand in your light.

lessons.title: David's Repentance
lessons.theme: True repentance does not save face; it asks God to create a new heart

v: Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions.
Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin.
For I know my transgressions. My sin is constantly before me.
Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.

lessons.still: Read Psalm 51:10 slowly, making it your own prayer. Then be still and place your hand over your heart. Don't ask God for a better performance; ask him for a clean heart.
teach: When ink stains a white shirt, you can't just spray perfume to cover the smell; the stain has to be thoroughly washed out. David committed adultery and murder and kept it hidden for a long time, until the prophet Nathan pointed at him and said, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). Psalm 51 is his prayer asking God to wash him completely clean.

David uses three words for sin: transgression (crossing the line in rebellion), iniquity (being twisted and bent), and sin (missing the mark). He also asks God for three actions: blot out, wash, cleanse. His appeal rests not on his own merit but on God's “loving kindness” and “the multitude of your tender mercies.” Above all, he asks God to “create” a clean heart — the same word as “created” in Genesis 1:1, something only God can do.

David's greatness was not that he never sinned, but that when confronted he did not defend himself or shift the blame. When Saul was rebuked, he said, “I have sinned; yet please honour me now before the elders of my people” (1 Samuel 15:30) — still concerned about saving face. True repentance is not sorrow over consequences but sorrow over grieving God's heart; not repairing our image, but asking God for a new heart.
lessons.light: 321 Light: David said, “Against you, and you only, have I sinned” (51:4); his focus was on God, not on his reputation. True repentance is turning from the self-ruled life to the self-emptied life — no longer protecting our image, only asking God to create us anew. Change the mindset and the life first, then the lifestyle: first a new heart, then new behaviour.
q: Who is God? — David asked forgiveness from a God of “loving kindness” and “tender mercies.” Is that the God you picture in your heart?
Who am I? — Is your repentance more like Saul's (concerned with face) or David's (concerned with God)?
How shall I respond? — In what area today will you ask God to “create in me a clean heart”?
lessons.jesus: Peter denied the Lord three times and went out and wept bitterly; by the lake, the risen Jesus asked him three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). The Lord was not shaming him but restoring him. Before Jesus, true repentance always leads to restoration.
lessons.pray: God, have mercy on me according to your loving kindness; according to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions. I will no longer defend my reputation; I simply confess that I have sinned against you. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Copy out Psalm 51:10 and put it somewhere you will see it often
When you are corrected, don't make excuses; just say, “Thank you for pointing that out”
Read 2 Samuel 12 and notice how David responds
lessons.noon: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.” — Lord, right now make me clean.

lessons.title: God Forgives Completely
lessons.theme: Because God's forgiveness is so complete, we can live free

v: He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.
For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his loving kindness toward those who fear him.
As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.
He will again have compassion on us. He will tread our iniquities under foot. You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

lessons.still: Imagine handing the Lord a stone with your sins written on it, and watching him throw it into the depths of the sea. The surface grows calm again. Quietly tell yourself, “It is forgiven.” Let those words settle in your heart.
teach: Someone once said that God throws our sins into the depths of the sea and then puts up a sign: “No Fishing.” Many Christians confess their sins yet keep going back to the shore to fish the old ones out and chew on them again. Yesterday we learned how to repent; today we see how complete God's forgiveness is.

Psalm 103 paints forgiveness in three pictures: God has not dealt with us “according to” our sins; his loving kindness is as high as the heavens above the earth; he removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west — travel north far enough and you start heading south, but travel east and you never reach the west. Micah adds two more pictures: he treads our iniquities “under foot” and casts them “into the depths of the sea.”

Refusing to accept forgiveness can look like humility, but it is actually hidden pride — as if the cross were not enough and needed my self-reproach to finish the job. Here is the change of mindset: my feelings cannot overturn God's declaration. Sometimes we still bear the consequences of sin, but its penalty has already been carried by Christ. Only those who have been forgiven have the strength to forgive others.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Letting God be God includes letting him be the God who forgives — accepting his verdict and no longer retrying the case ourselves. Focus on the precious blood of Jesus, not on your feelings. Gratitude for forgiveness gives the glory to Jesus and becomes the foundation for forgiving others.
q: Who is God? — “As far as the east is from the west” — how do you understand the distance of God's forgiveness?
Who am I? — Is there a sin you have already confessed that you keep “fishing back up”?
How shall I respond? — How will you declare and receive God's forgiveness today?
lessons.jesus: To the woman despised by everyone, who wet his feet with her tears, Jesus said, “Your sins are forgiven,” and then, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace” (Luke 7:48–50). The Lord's forgiveness not only removes sin; it gives peace.
lessons.pray: Loving Father, thank you for not dealing with me according to my sins. I give you the old sins I keep going back to, trusting that you have thrown them into the depths of the sea. I will no longer use self-reproach in place of the cross. Set me free in your forgiveness, and give me strength to forgive others. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down a sin you have already confessed, write “Forgiven” beside it, then tear it up
When an old sin resurfaces, declare: “As far as the east is from the west.”
Thank the Lord for three freedoms you have gained through being forgiven
lessons.noon: “As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.” — Lord, right now I live in your forgiveness.

lessons.title: Forgiving as the Lord Forgave Me
lessons.theme: Both the power and the measure of forgiveness come from God's forgiveness

v: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.still: Quietly let the name of someone who has hurt you come to mind. You don't need to do anything right away; just place them, together with your wound, before the Lord and say, “Lord, you forgave me. Please help me.”
teach: Forgiveness is like defusing a bomb: the bomb is still there and the harm was real, but it can no longer go off in your heart again and again. In the first stage we learned the line from the Lord's Prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” This week we face it more deeply: how do we truly forgive?

Peter thought forgiving seven times was generous. But Jesus said “seventy times seven” — not meaning we count to 490, but that we stop counting. Paul gives the measure of forgiveness: “just as God also in Christ forgave you.” The more clearly we see how great a debt we have been forgiven, the more we are able to forgive others.

Forgiveness does not mean saying the hurt didn't matter, nor restoring trust immediately, nor giving up on justice. Forgiveness means handing the authority to judge back to God and no longer acting as judge ourselves. Forgiveness often takes one decision, followed by many renewed choices. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on the person who hurt you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Refusing to forgive is sitting on the judgement seat, which is God's place; forgiving is laying down power and returning to our place, letting God be God. Pride stirs up pride, and revenge breeds revenge; humility draws out humility, and forgiveness opens the door for both sides to win. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than being right.
q: Who is God? — How great is the measure with which God forgave you in Christ?
Who am I? — Are you still keeping a ledger in your heart of what others owe you?
How shall I respond? — For whom will you say to God today, “I choose to forgive”?
lessons.jesus: As he was nailed to the cross, Jesus prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He forgave at the moment of greatest pain. That forgiving life now lives in us, making the impossible possible.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, on the cross you forgave those who crucified you, and you have forgiven me. I bring … before you, and I choose to stop being their judge and to leave justice in your hands. When I cannot do it, let your life within me do the forgiving. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down the person you need to forgive, and beside their name write, “I hand them to God's judgement”
Pray a blessing over that person, however short
Stop retelling the hurtful incident to other people
lessons.noon: “Forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” — Lord, right now I hand judgement over to you.

lessons.title: The Chains of Unforgiveness
lessons.theme: Unforgiveness tries to lock others up but locks us in first

v: Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.
Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’
His lord was angry, and delivered him to the tormentors until he should pay all that was due to him.
So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds.”
looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it,

lessons.still: Clench your fists and feel the tension. Then slowly open them, palms up. Tell the Lord, “I'm letting go. Please set me free.” Be still for a while, and let that release spread from your palms into your heart.
teach: It has been said that unforgiveness is like drinking poison yourself and waiting for the other person to die. In the parable, the servant forgiven ten thousand talents turns around and seizes by the throat a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii — and ends up handed over to the tormentors. Jesus uses this extreme contrast to show us that an unforgiving heart is itself a prison.

The master asks, “Shouldn't you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?” The key is “even as I.” When we forget how much grace we have received, we magnify what others owe us. Jesus speaks of forgiving “from your hearts,” not a surface reconciliation. Hebrews warns of a “root of bitterness”: bitterness grows underground, unseen, yet “springing up” it causes trouble and defiles many — one person's bitterness can poison an entire community.

Joseph was sold by his brothers, yet years later he said, “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). He could forgive because he saw God's sovereignty. Here is the change of mindset: from “He ruined my life” to “God works all things together for good.” This week we have learned confession and forgiveness; next week we learn to be filled with the Holy Spirit — only a heart that has been emptied can be filled.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others. Forgiven by God, we can accept ourselves; accepting ourselves, we can forgive others. Unforgiveness is a fortress of the self-ruled life; forgiveness is the release of the self-emptied life. The self-emptied life overcomes Satan — and bitterness is exactly the breach through which the enemy breaks into a community.
q: Who is God? — The master in the parable cancelled a debt of ten thousand talents. Have you experienced grace like that from God?
Who am I? — Is there a “root of bitterness” growing in your heart?
How shall I respond? — What action will you take today to “unclench your fists”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus knew Judas would betray him, yet he washed his feet and ate with him (John 13). Peter denied the Lord, yet the angel gave special instructions: “Go, tell his disciples and Peter” (Mark 16:7). In Jesus' heart there was no root of bitterness, only a wellspring of grace.
lessons.pray: Lord, you cancelled all my debt, yet I often cling to the small debts others owe me. I confess there is bitterness in my heart; please pull it out by the root. I choose to unclench my fists and hand that person and that matter over to you. Set me free, and make my heart a channel through which your grace can flow. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Read Genesis 50:15–21 and learn how Joseph saw God's sovereignty
Do a small act of kindness for someone who has wronged you
Share with a spiritual companion the lesson in forgiveness you are learning
lessons.noon: “Lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you and many be defiled by it” — Lord, right now pull out the bitterness in my heart.

mem.t: Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit,

lessons.title: The Spirit of Pentecost
lessons.theme: The Spirit came down, bringing God's presence to dwell in every believer

v: Now when the day of Pentecost had come, they were all with one accord in one place.
Suddenly there came from the sky a sound like the rushing of a mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting.
Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them.
They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak.

lessons.still: Breathe quietly, and consider that breath and wind are both invisible, yet real. Say to the Lord, “Holy Spirit, you already live in me.” Don't seek an unusual feeling; ask only to become more aware of his presence.
teach: However beautiful a sailing boat is, without wind it can only sit in the harbour; what the sailor can do is raise the sail and turn it to catch the wind. In the first stage we learned that the Holy Spirit lives in our hearts and that we are to live from the heart by the Spirit. This week we go a step further: being filled with the Spirit. We begin back at the starting point — Pentecost.

Pentecost was originally a harvest festival, when the firstfruits of the wheat were offered. When God came down on Mount Sinai there was thunder and fire; now the Spirit comes like a mighty wind and tongues of fire. The law was carved on tablets of stone, but the Spirit writes God's word on human hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; 2 Corinthians 3:3). The text says, “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit” — all of them, not a few spiritual elites.

The coming of the Spirit at Pentecost was a once-for-all event in the history of redemption, like the cross and the resurrection; yet in Acts, “being filled with the Spirit” happens again and again (Acts 4:8, 4:31). Here is the change of mindset: the Holy Spirit is not a force for us to use but a Person, God himself, who wants to direct us. The question is not “How much of the Spirit do I have?” but “How much of me does the Spirit have?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Among the three foundations is this: the Holy Spirit is my guide. Being filled is not chasing a feeling but yielding control — only the self-emptied life can be led by the Spirit. The path of service begins with “Spirit”: first the Spirit's guidance, then understanding of the truth, the life of Jesus, and true ministry.
q: Who is God? — The Spirit came like wind and fire. What does that show you about God's presence?
Who am I? — Do you tend to treat the Holy Spirit as a power, or as the Lord who wants to direct you?
How shall I respond? — In what matter today will you “raise your sail” and wait for the Spirit's guidance?
lessons.jesus: After Jesus was baptised, the Holy Spirit descended on him like a dove (Luke 3:22); “full of the Holy Spirit, he returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4:1) and began his ministry. If even the Son of God relied on the Spirit in his ministry on earth, how much more must we?
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, thank you for coming down at Pentecost and for living in me. I don't ask for an extraordinary experience; I ask only that you would have more of me. I raise the sail of my life — blow on me and guide me, and govern my thoughts, words and actions today. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Read Acts 2 and circle every mention of the Holy Spirit
Before making a decision, pause for three seconds and silently ask, “Holy Spirit, what do you want?”
Thank God for a past time when you experienced the Spirit's guidance
lessons.noon: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit.” — Lord, right now I open myself to your Spirit.

lessons.title: Signs of Being Filled
lessons.theme: The evidence of being filled with the Spirit is praise, thanksgiving and mutual submission

v: Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit,
speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father;
subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.

lessons.still: Hum a hymn or worship song you know well, aloud or in your heart. Let the words become a prayer. Then be still, and count three things you can give thanks for right now, naming them slowly one by one.
teach: When someone is drunk, everyone around can tell: their speech, their walk and their face are all under the control of alcohol. Paul contrasts being “drunken with wine” with being “filled with the Spirit.” In both cases a power takes control, but the results are opposite: wine leads to dissipation, while the Spirit makes us more and more like Christ.

After “be filled” in verse 18, the original text continues with several participles describing the life that naturally flows from a filled person: speaking to one another in psalms and hymns (building one another up in relationship), singing and making melody to the Lord (worship toward God), giving thanks to the Father for all things (our attitude toward circumstances), and submitting to one another in the fear of Christ (humility with others). Immediately after this, Paul turns to the relationships of husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and servants.

Many assume the sign of being filled with the Spirit must be some dramatic experience, but what Paul mentions first here is praise on our lips, thanksgiving in our hearts and submission in our relationships. Here is the change of mindset: the evidence of being filled shows up not only in church meetings, but even more at home, at work, and in how others experience us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The first sign of a Spirit-filled person is that Jesus is glorified; the last is mutual submission — humility draws out humility, and relationships become a win for both sides. Giving thanks in everything is the “God” step of the path of service: all glory to God. God's kingdom system is built in homes and churches like these.
q: Who is God? — The Spirit makes melody in our hearts. How does he long for us to relate to God?
Who am I? — What do others see in you more — being “filled with emotions” or being “filled with the Spirit”?
How shall I respond? — In which relationship today will you practise “subjecting yourselves to one another”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “rejoiced in the Holy Spirit” and gave thanks to the Father (Luke 10:21); he submitted to the Father and gladly served people. His whole life was one of praise, thanksgiving and submission — the most beautiful picture of a Spirit-filled life.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, fill me and govern me. May there be praise on my lips and thanksgiving in my heart, and may I submit to others in the fear of Christ, at home and at work. Do not let emotions or desires control me; let you control me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Sing or quietly recite at least one song of praise today
Before bed, write down five things you are thankful for, including one difficulty
At home or at work, choose once to defer to someone rather than push to be first
lessons.noon: “But be filled with the Spirit” — Lord, right now govern my heart and my lips.

lessons.title: Being Filled Is Ongoing Obedience
lessons.theme: Being filled is not a one-time experience but following him step by step

v: Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.
Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

lessons.still: Think back over today so far. Was there a moment of unease, as if you brushed past a gentle prompting? Quietly tell the Lord, “Holy Spirit, I'm sorry. I'm willing to obey right now.”
teach: Hold a cup under a tap upside down, and no matter how much water flows, none will go in. The key to being filled is not a shortage of water but the posture of the cup. In the original, “be filled” in Ephesians 5:18 is a present, passive command: keep on letting the Spirit fill you.

Galatians says that those who belong to Christ have “crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts”; since we “live by the Spirit,” we should also “walk by the Spirit.” The word for “walk” here carries the idea of falling into line and advancing step by step — keeping in step with the Spirit. Ephesians reminds us not to grieve the Spirit: he is a Person who can be grieved, not cold, impersonal energy.

What grieves the Spirit? The surrounding verses list lying, letting the sun go down on our anger, stealing, corrupt speech, bitterness and wrath (Ephesians 4:25–31). So last week's confession and forgiveness were exactly the preparation for being filled. Here is the change of mindset: we are filled not by chasing more but by obeying more — every act of obedience makes room for the Spirit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Living from the heart by the Spirit means obeying his promptings in small things; living from the head by yourself means hearing him but stopping to calculate first. Self-rule leads the march itself; self-emptying keeps in step behind the Spirit. Obedience is not losing freedom but entering the limitless.
q: Who is God? — The Spirit can be “grieved.” What does that reveal about God's heart?
Who am I? — Is there a recent prompting of the Spirit that you have still not obeyed?
How shall I respond? — What step of obedience will you take today to keep in step with the Spirit?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). Every step of his life was in step with the Father. He did not obey occasionally but continually — and that is the Spirit-filled life.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, I confess that I often grieve you, hearing your promptings and not obeying. Please forgive me. Today I want to follow you step by step and obey your promptings in small things. Keep on filling me and govern every part of my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Obey right away a prompting of the Spirit you have long put off
Today, notice a bitter word you're about to say, and choose not to say it
In the evening, review: which steps today kept in step with the Spirit, and where did I fall behind?
lessons.noon: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” — Lord, right now I keep in step with you.

lessons.title: Power for Witness
lessons.theme: The Spirit's power is not for ourselves but for bearing witness to Christ

v: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”
When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness.

lessons.still: Quietly bring to mind a relative or friend who does not yet know the Lord, and bring their name before him. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I am timid, but your Spirit is powerful. Please give me an opportunity, and give me courage.”
teach: Connect electricity to a light bulb and it shines; connect it to a motor and the machine turns — power always has a purpose. Before he ascended, Jesus promised his disciples, “You will receive power,” and immediately explained why: “You will be witnesses to me.” The Spirit's power is not for showing off our spiritual experiences but for letting Christ be seen.

Acts 1:8 sketches an ever-widening circle: from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth — which is also the outline of the whole book of Acts. In chapter 4, when Peter and John were threatened and ordered never again to speak in the name of Jesus, the church's response was not to ask for their enemies to disappear but to pray; and “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness.” One of the fruits of being filled is boldness.

This same Peter had once denied the Lord in front of a servant girl; filled with the Spirit, he boldly bore witness before the Council. His change came not from willpower but from the Holy Spirit. Here is the change of mindset: witnessing is not selling religion but telling what Jesus has done for me; my weakness is the very place where the Spirit's power is displayed.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Spirit's witness is focused on Jesus, not on the witness — this is letting Jesus receive all the glory. Of the five changes, “ministry” is built on “life” and “relationships”: first be filled, then bear witness; first live out Christ, then speak of Christ.
q: Who is God? — God promised power to timid disciples. What is his heart toward your weakness?
Who am I? — Who is in your “Jerusalem” — the harvest field nearest to you?
How shall I respond? — For whom will you ask today for an opportunity and the courage to bear witness?
lessons.jesus: In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read, “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to preach good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18). His power was always used to set people free, heal them and bring them back to the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I am often timid about bearing witness to you. Fill me with your Holy Spirit and give me courage and wisdom — not to show off myself, but so that people may see you. Give me an opportunity today to tell someone near me what you have done in my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down three people in your “Jerusalem” who don't yet believe
Pray for one of them, asking for a natural opportunity to share
Write “What Jesus has done for me” in three sentences
lessons.noon: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.” — Lord, right now make me bold to bear witness to you.

lessons.title: Asking to Be Filled Every Day
lessons.theme: Like drinking water when we are thirsty, we come to the Lord daily to receive the Spirit

v: If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”
Now on the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!
He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, from within him will flow rivers of living water.”

lessons.still: Feel your own thirst: weariness, emptiness, being stretched beyond your strength. Don't hide it; tell the Lord plainly, “Lord, I am thirsty.” Then, as if taking a drink of water, quietly receive: “I believe you are filling me right now.”
teach: No one can quench today's thirst with water drunk last week, and a phone can't last today on a charge from last month. Spiritual life is the same. Ephesians 5:18 is a continuous command, so being filled is not a certificate on file but something we receive every day.

On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus cried out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!” John goes on to explain that he was speaking of the Spirit whom those who believed in him would receive (7:39). The contrast in Luke 11:13 is simple: if even imperfect fathers give their children good things, “how much more” your heavenly Father? When we ask for the Spirit, we are not beggars pleading for scraps but children asking their Father.

This week we have seen that the Spirit of Pentecost has come; that the signs of being filled are praise, thanksgiving and submission; that being filled is ongoing obedience; and that power is for witness. Today we put it into a simple daily habit: each morning, admit your thirst, confess and be emptied, hand over control, and receive by faith. Next week we face a closely related subject: the root of pride and its remedy.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Asking to be filled every day is admitting that “apart from the Lord I can do nothing” — the prayer of the self-emptied life. Living from the head by yourself leaves you drier and drier; living from the heart by the Spirit lets living water well up. The rivers flowing out of us are meant to water our “2” and bear the ninefold fruit of the Spirit — this is 920.
q: Who is God? — “How much more your heavenly Father” — do you believe God is glad to give you the Holy Spirit?
Who am I? — How high is your spiritual “water level” right now? What is making you thirsty?
How shall I respond? — At what moment each day will you build the habit of asking to be filled?
lessons.jesus: Jesus often withdrew to the wilderness to pray (Luke 5:16). Even the Son of God needed daily fellowship with the Father, receiving from him. At the well he told the Samaritan woman that the water he gives becomes a spring within (John 4:14) — and that spring wells up toward us today.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, I confess that I am thirsty; on my own I have run dry. I come before you, confess my sins, hand over my control, and by faith receive the Holy Spirit you have promised. Fill me today, and let living water flow out from me to refresh the people around me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Tomorrow morning, make your first act a one-sentence prayer to be filled with the Spirit
Write “Admit thirst, confess, hand over, receive” on a sticky note
Memorise this week's verse: Ephesians 5:18
lessons.noon: “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink!” — Lord, right now I come to drink your living water.

mem.t: Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility and subject yourselves to one another; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

lessons.title: The Many Faces of Pride
lessons.theme: Pride wears a thousand disguises, but it has one root: self-centredness

v: Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.
For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?

lessons.still: Ask the Holy Spirit, like a doctor holding a magnifying glass, to examine your heart gently: “Lord, show me the pride in me that is hard to detect.” Wait quietly. Don't rush to defend yourself; just note the first picture that comes to mind.
teach: What makes a virus so hard to guard against is that it mutates: it changes its outward form while its nature stays the same. Pride is like that. In the first stage we learned that pride is leaving our place and grasping power. Last week we asked to be filled with the Spirit, and pride is the number one obstacle to the Spirit. Today we learn to recognise pride's many variants, because the most dangerous pride is often the kind we fail to recognise.

Paul asked the self-important Corinthians three questions: Who makes you different? What do you have that you didn't receive? And if you received it, why do you boast? These three questions demolish every foundation of pride — everything we have, we have received. Proverbs warns: pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.

Pride has obvious faces: boasting, looking down on others, refusing to be taught, needing to control. It also has hidden faces: self-pity (“Nobody understands me”), excessive self-blame (“How could I have failed?”), people-pleasing (caring too much about our image), and spiritual superiority. They all have one root: being centred on self. Eyes held high and eyes cast down may both be looking only at ourselves.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our place and grasping power — wanting to be our own god, and other people's god too. Pride is the outward expression of the self-ruled life; only by recognising its many disguises can we treat it properly. Humility is the key to revival, and that key begins with honestly seeing ourselves.
q: Who is God? — “What do you have that you didn't receive?” What does this show you about God as the Giver?
Who am I? — Which face of pride shows up most often in you: boasting, controlling, self-pity, or people-pleasing?
How shall I respond? — When that face appears today, how will you recognise it and hand it to the Lord?
lessons.jesus: On earth, Jesus spoke of everything as received: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7:16). He possessed everything yet took no credit; we have nothing of our own, yet often want the credit. He is the perfect pattern of the self-emptied life.
lessons.pray: Lord, search me and show me the disguised pride in my heart: boasting, controlling, self-pity, people-pleasing. I confess that everything I have, I have received from you, and I have nothing to boast about. Tear down my self-centredness and bring me back to my place. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down the face of pride that shows up most often in you, and what triggers it
Today, change one “I did it” into “Thank you, Lord, for enabling me to do it”
Ask a trusted companion to tell you one blind spot they see in you
lessons.noon: “And what do you have that you didn’t receive?” — Lord, right now I acknowledge that everything comes from you.

lessons.title: Two Men Who Prayed
lessons.theme: God looks not at the length of a prayer but at the heart of the one praying

v: “Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed by himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

lessons.still: Be still for a moment in the posture of the tax collector: bow your head, with no need to find any reason to score points for yourself. Come before God with a single sentence: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” Repeat it slowly, and let your heart catch up with your lips.
teach: Two men stood in the same temple doing the same thing — praying — yet the outcomes were worlds apart. Jesus told this parable “to certain people who were convinced of their own righteousness, and who despised all others” (18:9). The sharpest point of the parable is this: after reading it, it is very easy to think, “Thank God I'm not like that Pharisee” — and in that moment we have become the Pharisee.

The Pharisee “prayed to himself” — on the surface he was speaking to God, but really he was talking to himself. Every line of his prayer revolves around “I,” focused entirely on his own performance and other people's failures. The tax collector stood “far away” and “beat his breast,” asking only for mercy. The word “be merciful” is linked to the Old Testament mercy seat and atonement: he was asking for God's covering, not God's approval.

Religious pride is the hardest to cure, because it wears spiritual clothing. If our Bible reading, prayer and giving become capital for comparing ourselves with others, they turn from channels of grace into stepping stones of pride. Here is the change of mindset: the purpose of spiritual disciplines is not to make me better than others, but to make me more dependent on God and closer to him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Pharisee's focus was on himself and on others; the tax collector's focus was on God. “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted” is the spiritual law of humility. Let God be God: only he can justify, so I don't need to justify myself.
q: Who is God? — What does the God who justified the tax collector value in a person?
Who am I? — Have your spiritual disciplines ever quietly become capital for comparing yourself with others?
How shall I respond? — Which posture of the tax collector will you take as you come before God today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners and was criticised for it (Luke 15:1–2). He said, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5:32). In his presence, those who admit their need are the first to receive grace.
lessons.pray: God, be merciful to me, a sinner! I lay down my spiritual résumé and stop using others' failures to make myself look good. I confess that I need your covering and your mercy. Do not let my Bible reading and prayer become stepping stones of pride, but a deeper dependence on you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: When you pray today, don't mention what you have done; simply ask the Lord for mercy
When you catch yourself comparing with someone in your heart, immediately bless that person
Notice how many times the word “I” appears in your prayers
lessons.noon: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” — Lord, right now I look only to your mercy.

lessons.title: Nebuchadnezzar Humbled
lessons.theme: God can humble the proud, and he can restore the humble

v: The king spoke and said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?”
Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven; for all his works are truth, and his ways justice; and those who walk in pride he is able to abase.

lessons.still: Lift your eyes to heaven, as Nebuchadnezzar did when he was restored. Say to the Lord, “You are the King of heaven; I am your creature.” Quietly place the achievement you are proudest of back into the Lord's hands.
teach: A great tree grows until it reaches the sky and begins to think it is holding the sky up. That is exactly the tree Nebuchadnezzar saw in his dream — cut down, with only the stump left (Daniel 4). A year later, walking on the roof of his palace, he boasted, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built…?” — and while the words were still in his mouth, judgement fell.

This chapter traces a turning line through the word “I.” In verse 30: “the might of my power,” “the glory of my majesty” — all the credit goes to himself. In verse 34: “I lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me” — his turning begins with looking up. In verse 37: “I… praise and extol and honor the King of heaven” — the same “I,” but now focused on God. Pride made him like a beast; humility restored him to being human.

God humbles the proud not to destroy them but to restore them: leaving the stump means leaving hope. Sometimes God allows us to lose health, position or plans so that we may know that “the Most High rules in the kingdom of men” (4:25). Here is the change of mindset: when you are humbled, don't only ask “Why?” — ask even more, “Lord, what place do you want me to return to?”
