lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our human place and wanting to be God — and ending up unable even to be human. Humility is returning to our place: letting people be people and letting God be God. In the end Nebuchadnezzar gave all praise, honour and glory to the King of heaven — this is letting God receive all the glory.
q: Who is God? — “The Most High rules in the kingdom of men.” What does this mean for your situation today?
Who am I? — Is there a “great Babylon” in your life that you secretly believe you built yourself?
How shall I respond? — How will you “lift your eyes to heaven” today and give the glory to God?
lessons.jesus: Nebuchadnezzar tried to rise from man to god and sank to the level of a beast; Jesus, existing in the form of God, humbled himself to become man, and God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:9). The way of pride is grasping upward and falling; the way of humility is stooping downward and being lifted up.
lessons.pray: King of heaven, you rule in the kingdom of men. I confess that I have taken the achievements you gave me as my own credit. I lift my eyes to heaven and give all praise, honour and glory to you. If you need to humble me, please also restore me, and bring me back to my place as a human being. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Pick one of your achievements and write down every part of it that you “received”
When someone praises you, name specifically the help you had from God or from others
Read Daniel 4 and notice God's patience and his warnings
lessons.noon: “And those who walk in pride he is able to abase.” — Lord, right now I humble myself before you.

lessons.title: Clothed with Humility
lessons.theme: Humility is not a passing posture but clothing we put on every day

v: Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility and subject yourselves to one another; for “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time,
casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

lessons.still: Picture yourself getting dressed in the morning and, last of all, tying on an apron. Say to the Lord, “Lord, today I clothe myself with humility.” Then take one thing that is worrying you and, like slipping off a heavy backpack, cast it onto him.
teach: In ancient times, servants tied a cloth around their waist before working, so their clothes wouldn't get in the way and they were ready to serve. The word Peter uses for “clothe yourselves” paints exactly this picture: tying on a servant's apron. Humility is not a posture we strike now and then, but work clothes we put on every day. Perhaps Peter remembered the night the Lord “took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist” and knelt to wash his feet.

Verse 5 is addressed to “all of you”: the younger submit to the elder, and everyone submits to one another. The reason: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” In verse 6, “humble yourselves” means actively placing ourselves under God's mighty hand; in verse 7, “casting all your worries on him” is trust shown in action. The proud carry everything themselves; the humble hand their worries to the God who cares for them.

Humility faces two directions. Toward God, it means placing ourselves under his mighty hand and casting our worries on him; toward others, it means submitting to one another and gladly serving. The two are closely linked: those who will not hand their worries to God often try to control people. Here is the change of mindset: humility is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less, and of God and others more.
lessons.light: 321 Light: “God resists the proud” — pride puts us in a position of opposition to God. “He gives grace to the humble” — humility is the channel through which grace flows in, which is why humility is the key to revival. When I lay down power, return to my place, cast my worries on God and let God be God, I am set free.
q: Who is God? — “He cares for you.” How does this God regard your worries?
Who am I? — Is your humility more like a one-time posture or something you put on daily?
How shall I respond? — Whom will you “tie on the apron” to serve today, and what worry will you cast onto God?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist” and knelt to wash his disciples' feet (John 13:4–5). He was Lord, yet he put on a servant's work clothes. Peter protested at the time, but later he wrote, “clothe yourselves with humility” — he finally understood that the towel was meant for every follower.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you once wrapped a towel around your waist and washed my feet. Today I too want to clothe myself with humility and place myself under God's mighty hand. I cast the worries of my heart on you, because you care for me. Make me glad to submit and glad to serve, and let me receive the grace you give to the humble. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: As you dress in the morning, pray silently: “Lord, today I clothe myself with humility.”
Take on a serving task that someone else usually does
Memorise this week's verse: 1 Peter 5:5
lessons.noon: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” — Lord, right now I clothe myself with humility.

lessons.title: Humility Meets Humility
lessons.theme: Only when we answer pride with humility can relationships become a win for both sides

v: Be of the same mind one toward another. Don’t set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble. Don’t be wise in your own conceits.
A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

lessons.still: Recall a person or situation that recently made you want to “hit back.” Don't think yet about what to say; just tell the Lord quietly, “Lord, let me be humble first.” Take three deep breaths, and with each one lay down a little more of the urge to win.
teach: When two people meet in a narrow alley, if both push forward with chests out, they collide; if one turns sideways to make room, the other usually turns sideways too. Pride stirs up pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. This is a principle we learned in the first stage; today we carry it into our most real conflicts.

Romans 12:16 has two “don'ts” and one “but”: don't set your mind on high things, don't be wise in your own conceits, but associate with the humble — all of them deal with the posture of putting ourselves above others in relationships. Proverbs 15:1 shows the chain reaction of words: a gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. A single sentence can start a fire, or put one out.

Humility meeting humility does not mean waiting for the other person to be humble first; it means I go first. When someone treats me with pride, if I respond with pride, it becomes self-rule against self-rule; if I respond with humility, I open the door for the Holy Spirit to work. This week we have seen the root, the faces and the remedy of pride; next week we face temptation — and pride is the very breach temptation most often exploits.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility draws out humility, and both sides win. This is also how God's kingdom system is built: not by anyone beating anyone else, but by stooping low for one another and building one another up. In 920, every “2” is someone with whom I practise the “0” of the self-emptied life, bearing the fruit of gentleness, patience and peace.
q: Who is God? — How does the God who associates with the humble treat you in your lowliness?
Who am I? — When faced with someone else's pride, how do you most often “hit back”?
How shall I respond? — With which of your “2” will you lead with a gentle answer today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus, “when he was cursed, didn't curse back. When he suffered, didn't threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously” (1 Peter 2:23). His gentleness was not weakness but a greater strength, which in the end overcame human pride and the schemes of Satan.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, when you were cursed you did not curse back, but entrusted yourself to the Father who judges righteously. In conflict, keep me from answering pride with pride; help me to be humble first and gentle first. Teach me to associate with the humble and not be wise in my own eyes. May my humility draw out humility in others, so that you receive the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: In a conversation that could become an argument, lower your voice and slow your speech first
Say to one of your “2”: “I was partly in the wrong in this too.”
Share with a spiritual companion one kind of pride you recognised in yourself this week
lessons.noon: “A gentle answer turns away wrath.” — Lord, right now let me be humble first.

mem.t: No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.

lessons.title: Where Temptation Comes From
lessons.theme: Only when we see where temptation comes from can we avoid being dragged along by it

v: Let no man say when he is tempted, “I am tempted by God,” for God can’t be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.
But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.
Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.
For all that is in the world— the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life—isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.

lessons.still: Quietly ask the Lord to shine his light: “Lord, at what times, in what places, in what moods am I most likely to fall?” Don't carry shame — just be honest, like a patient describing symptoms to a doctor.
teach: An angler never lets the fish see the hook, only the bait. The word James uses for “enticed” originally carries the idea of luring with bait. He describes a clear chain: lust draws us away and entices us → it conceives and gives birth to sin → sin grows up and produces death. Sin does not happen suddenly; it grows step by step.

James first rules out an excuse: “I am tempted by God.” God does test people so that their faith may grow, but he never entices anyone to sin. The root of the problem lies in “each one… his own lust.” John names the world's three enticements: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life — matching exactly the fruit in Eden, which was “good for food,” “a delight to the eyes” and “to be desired to make one wise.”

Temptation has three sources: the world around us, the flesh within us and the devil behind it all. But what Satan can exploit is always the “self” within us — the self-ruled life is the breach in the wall. Here is the change of mindset: being tempted is not sin — Jesus was tempted too; giving in to temptation is sin. The earlier we cut the chain, the easier it is to overcome.
lessons.light: 321 Light: “The pride of life” links last week to this week: at the heart of temptation is usually the self-ruled life — wanting to be in charge of ourselves and satisfy ourselves. The self-emptied life overcomes Satan, because there is no “self” for him to grab hold of. When our focus is on Jesus, the bait loses its pull.
q: Who is God? — “God can't be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.” How does this help you trust his intentions?
Who am I? — Which temptation drags you along most easily: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, or the pride of life?
How shall I respond? — At which link in the chain will you cut temptation off early?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “The prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30). Satan could find nothing in Jesus to grab hold of, because Jesus was completely self-emptied and completely obedient to the Father. This Lord lives in us, and he is the source of our victory.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that temptation often begins with my own desires. Shine your light on the places where I easily fall, so that I recognise desire as soon as it sprouts and hand it over to you. I don't want to be drawn by the bait, only drawn to you. Reign in me, and give the enemy no foothold. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down the times, places and moods in which you are most easily tempted
Set up a line of defence — for example, no more scrolling your phone after a certain time at night
When temptation surfaces, say at once: “This is bait, not blessing.”
lessons.noon: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed.” — Lord, right now I turn my eyes to you.

lessons.title: Victory in the Wilderness
lessons.theme: As a man, Jesus overcame temptation by the word of God

v: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.
When he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was hungry afterward.
The tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.”
But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’”
For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin.

lessons.still: Picture Jesus in the wilderness — hungry and alone, yet standing firm. Say to the Lord, “Lord, you understand my weakness.” Tell him where you feel weakest right now, and let his sympathy catch you.
teach: The first Adam fell in a garden of plenty; Jesus, the last Adam, overcame in a barren wilderness. Israel failed again and again during forty years in the wilderness; Jesus, through forty days and nights in the wilderness, did not fail. He walked again the road where humanity had failed — and he won.

The key to the first temptation is “If you are the Son of God” — just one chapter earlier the Father had declared, “This is my beloved Son” (3:17). Satan attacked his identity, enticing Jesus to use his own power to meet his own needs and step out of dependence on the Father. Jesus answered with Deuteronomy 8:3; all three times he said, “It is written.” As a man, he overcame by the Holy Spirit and the word of God.

Satan's temptations often work on three levels: doubting our identity (Are you really God's child?), satisfying ourselves (No need to wait for God), and taking a shortcut to glory (No need to carry a cross). Jesus' responses teach us that our identity is confirmed by God's word, our needs are met by waiting on God, and the glory belongs to God alone. Hebrews says he was “in all points tempted,” so he can sympathise with us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The three foundations shine out fully in the wilderness: the Spirit led Jesus (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Jesus answered with Scripture (Scripture is my standard), and Jesus refused to use his authority for himself (Jesus is my example). Here we see most clearly how the self-emptied life overcomes Satan.
q: Who is God? — How does the High Priest who was “in all points tempted like we are” regard your struggles?
Who am I? — In what area does Satan most often attack your identity?
How shall I respond? — In what matter today will you “wait for God to provide” instead of grabbing for yourself?
lessons.jesus: Jesus could have commanded the stones to become bread, but he chose to depend on the Father in his hunger. Later he fed five thousand with five loaves and two fish — not for himself, but for others. He never used his power to serve himself, only to accomplish the Father's will and meet people's needs.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you overcame in the wilderness for me, and you sympathise with my weakness. When the enemy questions my identity, remind me that I am a child of the heavenly Father. Teach me not to take shortcuts or grab for myself, but to depend only on every word that proceeds out of your mouth. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Read Matthew 4:1–11 and write down the three temptations and the three responses
Today, choose to wait a little over something you want to satisfy “right now”
When temptation comes, say “It is written,” followed by a verse you have memorised
lessons.noon: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.” — Lord, right now I live by your word.

lessons.title: The Sword of the Spirit
lessons.theme: Hiding God's word in our hearts is our weapon against temptation

v: How can a young man keep his way pure? By living according to your word.
With my whole heart I have sought you. Don’t let me wander from your commandments.
I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.
And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God;

lessons.still: Choose a verse you already know by heart and repeat it slowly in your mind three times. Each time, imagine it dropping from your head into your heart, like a sword slipping into its sheath, ready to be drawn at any moment.
teach: A soldier doesn't wait until the enemy is charging at him to go looking for a sword and learn how to use it. Jesus could quote Deuteronomy on the spot in the wilderness because Scripture was already hidden in his heart. In the first stage we learned meditation and memorisation; today we see that the verses we memorise are the weapons in our hands in spiritual battle.

The psalmist asks how a young man can keep his way pure; the answer is “by living according to your word.” His method is to “hide” it in his heart — like treasure stored in a secret room — “that I might not sin against you.” Paul says “the sword of the Spirit… is the spoken word of God”: the word here often refers to a word that is spoken. This sword is the short blade used in close combat, and the only offensive weapon in the whole armour of God.

Notice: it is the sword “of the Spirit.” Scripture is not a magic spell; memorising more does not automatically mean victory — Satan quotes Scripture too (Matthew 4:6). The key is to use God's word by the Spirit and in obedience. Here is the change of mindset: we memorise Scripture not to pass a test but so that, in the moment of temptation, God's word speaks louder than our desires.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard and the Holy Spirit is my guide — the two come together in “the sword of the Spirit.” Live from the head by yourself, and memorising Scripture remains mere knowledge; live from the heart by the Spirit, and hiding the word becomes life. The “Repetition” step in the eight steps to changing our mindset means hiding the word in our hearts again and again.
q: Who is God? — What is the heart of a God who gives us his word as a weapon for our battles?
Who am I? — How many verses have you “hidden” in your heart? When temptation comes, which one can you draw?
How shall I respond? — For your most common temptation, which verse will you memorise as your sword?
lessons.jesus: Satan quoted a psalm out of context, and Jesus answered, “Again, it is written…” (Matthew 4:7). He didn't just quote Scripture; he knew how to use God's word according to the true meaning of the whole Bible. Finally he said, “Get behind me, Satan!” (Matthew 4:10). God's word drove the enemy away.
lessons.pray: Lord, your word is a lamp to my feet and a sword in my hand. Help me to hide your word in my heart, not just store it in my head. When temptation comes, Holy Spirit, bring the right verse to mind, so that I can draw the sword and overcome through you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Choose a verse that addresses your most common temptation and copy it onto a card
Recite this verse to yourself at least five times today
Tell the verse to a spiritual companion and ask them to test you on it later
lessons.noon: “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” — Lord, right now let your word speak in my heart.

lessons.title: Flee Youthful Lusts
lessons.theme: Some temptations are not to be resisted head-on but fled from

v: Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts.

lessons.still: Think honestly: in your life, which door, which setting, which app is often your entry point to falling? Quietly hand it over to the Lord: “Lord, give me the courage to close this door.”
teach: When there is a fire, firefighters rush in to put it out, but everyone else should run out. Scripture teaches us to “resist the devil,” and it also teaches us to “flee” from lust. Not every temptation is meant to be met head-on; with some, the way to overcome is to leave the scene.

Day after day Joseph was pressed by his master's wife. He said, “How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” In the end he left his garment in her hand and ran outside (Genesis 39). Paul tells Timothy to “flee,” and at the same time to “pursue” righteousness, faith, love and peace — “with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.” We are not meant to fight alone. Romans adds: “make no provision for the flesh” — don't leave a back door open in advance.

The self-ruled life often overestimates itself: “That won't happen to me; I'm standing firm.” That is actually pride. Humble people admit their weakness, so they set up defences early, flee when needed and find others to walk with them. Here is the change of mindset: running away is not cowardice but wisdom; setting boundaries is not legalism but a protection born of love for the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: In the face of temptation, humility looks like admitting, “I'm not strong enough,” and so we flee and ask for help. The spiritual companions in 235 are exactly those “who call on the Lord out of a pure heart,” pursuing alongside us. Putting on Christ means letting Jesus reign, not letting our desires reign.
q: Who is God? — How does the God who gave Joseph strength to turn and run also keep you in your situation?
Who am I? — Have you overestimated your ability to resist a particular temptation?
How shall I respond? — What door that “makes provision for the flesh” will you close today?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane Jesus told his disciples, “Watch and pray, that you don't enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41). He understands human weakness, so he calls us not to act tough but to watch, pray and walk together.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I am weaker than I think. Give me Joseph's courage to turn and run in the face of temptation. I am willing to close the doors that make provision for the flesh, and to put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Give me companions who call on you with a pure heart, so that together we pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Remove one entry point that often leads you to fall (an app, a bookmark, a route)
Invite a spiritual companion to keep watch with you in this area
Set one specific boundary, and write it down
lessons.noon: “Flee from youthful lusts.” — Lord, right now give me the courage to turn away.

lessons.title: God Will Make a Way Out
lessons.theme: The faithful God will not let us be tempted beyond what we can bear

v: Therefore let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall.

No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
For in that he himself has suffered being tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.

lessons.still: Recall a time when God made a way out for you in temptation, and quietly thank him for it. Then lay your present temptation before him: “Lord, you are faithful. Please show me the way out.”
teach: A maze looks like walls on every side, but the person who designed it knows there is always an exit. Paul says that with the temptation God “will also make the way of escape.” This does not mean temptation won't come; it means temptation never comes without an exit.

Verse 12 first warns, “let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn't fall.” The context is Israel's failure in the wilderness: they had seen miracles and eaten manna, yet still fell in the desert. Verse 13 then comforts: temptation is only “what is common to man”; “God is faithful” — there are limits and there is a way out, so “that you may be able to endure it.” Hebrews says that Jesus himself suffered when tempted, so he is able to help those who are tempted.

The way out is often very ordinary: shutting the computer, leaving the room, making a phone call, starting to pray, speaking a verse aloud. Often the problem is not that there is no way out but that we don't want to take it. This week we have looked at the source of temptation, Jesus' victory, the word of God, the wisdom of fleeing and the faithfulness of God. Many temptations slip in when we are idle and drifting; next week we will learn that our time belongs to God.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Victory does not depend on how firmly I stand but on God being faithful — the focus is on Jesus, not on our own strength. The humble can see the way out; the proud cannot, because they don't think they need one. The self-emptied life overcomes Satan: when we let Jesus reign, he himself is our way out.
q: Who is God? — “God is faithful.” How have you experienced his faithfulness in temptation?
Who am I? — In what area do you “think you stand”?
How shall I respond? — The next time temptation comes, what specific way out will you take?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said to Peter, “Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat, but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn't fail” (Luke 22:31–32). Though Peter fell, the Lord's intercession kept him so that he turned back. The Lord himself is the way out.
lessons.pray: Faithful God, thank you that you will not let me be tempted beyond what I can bear. I confess that I often think I'm standing firm; make me careful. When temptation comes, open my eyes to see the way out, and give me a heart willing to take it. Lord Jesus, you are my way out. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: For your most common temptation, write down three specific ways out in advance
Recall a time God made a way out for you, and give thanks for it
Memorise this week's verse: 1 Corinthians 10:13
lessons.noon: “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able.” — Lord, right now I trust that you will make a way out.

mem.t: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.

lessons.title: Time Is a Trust from God
lessons.theme: My time is not my property but something my Master has entrusted to me

v: But I trust in you, LORD. I said, “You are my God.”
My times are in your hand. Deliver me from the hand of my enemies, and from those who persecute me.
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.

lessons.still: Open today's calendar, or walk through the hours of today in your mind from morning to night. Then rest your hands open on your knees and say slowly, “Lord, my times are in your hand, and these twenty-four hours are yours too.”
teach: A steward who carries the keys to his master's house in and out every day can easily forget, over time, that the keys are not his own. We do the same with time. We say “my time” and “my weekend,” as if time were property we had earned. In fact, every morning when we wake, God places a fresh trust into our hands.

Hunted by his enemies, David said, “My times are in your hand.” He acknowledged that God is sovereign over time. The Preacher also says that God “has made everything beautiful in its time” and “has also set eternity in their hearts” — we live within limited time, yet our hearts long for eternity. Time is the stage God designed so that finite people might come to know the eternal God.

Change your mindset and you change your life: move from “Who has taken my time?” to “How does my Master want me to use his time today?” The first makes us grudging and restless; the second gives us rest and focus. A steward doesn't need to own, only to be faithful; he doesn't need to control everything, only to give an account to his master.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Saying “My time is mine to run” is the self-ruled life at work — making ourselves king over the twenty-four hours of the day. Handing time back to God means returning to our place as stewards and letting Jesus reign over our calendar; and the fruit of faithful use gives the glory to him as well.
q: Who is God? — “My times are in your hand.” How does this show you that God governs your days?
Who am I? — Do you tend to see your time as “my property” or as “my Master's trust”?
How shall I respond? — Which part of today will you deliberately use with a steward's heart?
lessons.jesus: At twelve years old Jesus said, “Didn't you know that I must be in my Father's house?” His life was not long, yet he was never in a rush, because he knew every moment belonged to the Father. He often said, “My hour has not yet come,” and later, “The hour has come” — he lived by the Father's timetable.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I often treat time as my own — impatient when I'm interrupted, and blaming myself when I waste it. Today I give this day back to you; I am your steward, not the master. Teach me to use faithfully every moment you entrust to me, so that you receive the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: At the top of today's calendar, write: “This day belongs to the Lord”
When someone interrupts you, first pray silently, “This is your time too,” and then respond
Before bed, spend three minutes giving the Lord an account of how you used today's time
lessons.noon: “My times are in your hand.” — Lord, right now I place this afternoon in your hands too.

lessons.title: Redeeming the Time
lessons.theme: Buying back for the Lord the time this evil age has taken from us

v: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise,
redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
Therefore, don’t be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time.

lessons.still: Be still for one minute and do nothing at all; just notice these sixty seconds slowly passing. Then ask the Lord, “Lord, what most often steals my time?” Don't rush to answer; let the Holy Spirit gently point it out.
teach: Someone pawns a family heirloom, then afterwards scrimps and saves to buy it back bit by bit. The phrase Paul uses, “redeeming the time,” carries exactly this sense of buying back. Time is God's treasure, but it so often gets pawned — to sin, to trivia, to endless scrolling on our phones — and we are to buy it back.

Here Paul contrasts two kinds of people: the unwise and the wise, the foolish and those who understand the Lord's will. Wisdom does not lie in how full we pack our schedule but in “understanding what the will of the Lord is.” In Colossians he is more specific: walk in wisdom toward outsiders. Redeeming the time often means seizing the moments when we meet people and can bear witness for the Lord.

Redeeming the time does not mean turning ourselves into efficiency machines; it means shifting the focus of our time from ourselves to the Lord. The question is not “How much more can I get done?” but “What does the Lord want me to do in this moment?” Sometimes the Lord's will is work; sometimes it is being present with someone; sometimes it is rest.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard: “understanding the will of the Lord” is the measure for how I arrange my time — not my preferences or other people's expectations. Focus on Jesus, not on the pressure of circumstances. We buy back time in order to let Jesus reign, not to prove how capable we are.
q: Who is God? — God wants us to “understand what the will of the Lord is.” What does this tell you about how much he cares about your day?
Who am I? — What most often “pawns” your time?
How shall I respond? — Which stretch of time will you buy back today and give to the Lord?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus met the Samaritan woman at the well, the disciples were busy buying food, but he seized the moment of that encounter. He said, “Lift up your eyes, and look at the fields, that they are white for harvest already.” His eyes could always see, in ordinary moments, what God was doing.
lessons.pray: Lord, forgive me for letting so much time be stolen by trivia and selfish desires. I want to be wise and understand your will. Open my eyes to every opportunity to meet people today, and help me to seize it with wisdom and gracious words, bearing witness to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Check your phone's screen-time report and honestly face one number
Take a stretch of time you would usually spend scrolling and use it to read the Bible or greet someone instead
In today's conversations, ask the Lord to help you say one word that builds someone up
lessons.noon: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” — Lord, right now I buy back this stretch of time and give it to you.

lessons.title: Numbering Our Days
lessons.theme: Only when we see how brief life is can we gain a heart of wisdom

v: So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.
Yet you don’t know what your life will be like tomorrow. For what is your life? For you are a vapor that appears for a little time and then vanishes away.
For you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will both live, and do this or that.”

lessons.still: Breathe in slowly, then breathe out slowly, and notice how the breath disperses like mist. Quietly say to the Lord, “Lord, my life is as brief as a vapour, but you are the everlasting God.” Let that contrast humble your heart.
teach: On a winter morning, breathe on a window and the white mist vanishes in a moment. James says our life is like that. This is not pessimism but clear-headedness. Someone who knows the sand is running through the hourglass will not waste their best time on things that don't matter.

Psalm 90 is a prayer of Moses. He first looks up to the God who is “from everlasting to everlasting,” then looks down at human beings, who are like grass, like a passing sleep. So he does not ask for a long life; he asks, “teach us to count our days.” The fruit of numbering our days is “a heart of wisdom” — and wisdom is not knowing more but living with the right priorities.

James rebukes those who say, “Tomorrow we will go into this city and trade,” not because planning is wrong, but because they have left God out of their plans. “If the Lord wills” is not a pious catchphrase but a change of mindset: from temporary to eternal, from my plans to God's will.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of perspective — from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal. Those living the self-ruled life assume tomorrow is in their own hands; those living the self-emptied life say, “If the Lord wills,” returning to their place as creatures and letting God be God. This is humility, and it is also wisdom.
q: Who is God? — The everlasting God watches over people as brief as a vapour. What does this show you about him?
Who am I? — In your plans, how much is “If the Lord wills” and how much is “I've decided”?
How shall I respond? — If you had only one year left, what would you stop, and what would you start?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. The night is coming, when no one can work.” He knew his days on earth were limited, so he walked single-mindedly in the Father's will and was never pulled along by the crowd's expectations.
lessons.pray: Everlasting God, teach me to number my days. My life is a vapour, but you are from everlasting to everlasting. Take away the pride that thinks I can hold tomorrow in my hands, and teach me to say “If the Lord wills” in every plan, so that I may gain a heart of wisdom. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Work out how many days you have lived so far, and give thanks for them
Next to one of this week's plans, write “If the Lord wills”
Write down one thing you keep putting off that has eternal significance
lessons.noon: “So teach us to count our days.” — Lord, right now give me a heart of wisdom.

lessons.title: Seek First His Kingdom
lessons.theme: When our priorities are right, everything else finds its place

v: But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.
Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.still: Draw an empty jar on a piece of paper. Quietly ask the Lord, “Lord, what is today's big rock?” Wait a moment, and write whatever the Holy Spirit brings to mind at the very bottom of the jar.
teach: If you want to fit big rocks, pebbles and sand into a jar, the order decides everything. Put the sand in first and the big rocks won't fit; put the big rocks in first and the pebbles and sand can fill in the gaps. The time of our lives works the same way: often the problem is not too little time but the wrong order.

Jesus said “seek first,” not “seek only.” He didn't say food, drink and clothing don't matter; he said the Father knows we need them and “all these things will be given to you as well.” Martha was not doing anything bad — she was serving Jesus. But she was “anxious and troubled about many things” and missed the “one thing” that “is needed.” The greatest danger is often not bad things, but good things in the wrong order.

In 321, the order of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, then with tasks. Meeting with God first each day is not adding one more chore; it is putting the big rock in first. When that rock is in the right place, everything else falls into order, and “each day's own evil is sufficient” no longer crushes us.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Seeking his kingdom first means letting Jesus reign. When ministry is put ahead of God and people, we end up hurting people for the sake of tasks. Life first, then relationships, then ministry — people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. When the order is right, life moves from anxiety to peace.
q: Who is God? — “Your heavenly Father knows.” What can this Father free you to lay down?
Who am I? — Are you more like Martha or Mary? Which “good thing” is in the wrong order?
How shall I respond? — Tomorrow morning, what big rock will you put into the jar first?
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “Your will be done.” The order of his life was never reversed: first the Father, then his disciples and the crowds, and only then the work. Because he was with the Father first, he still had time in his crowded schedule to stop and touch a man with leprosy.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, I am often anxious and troubled about many things, and I squeeze you to the very end. Today I want to seek first your kingdom and your righteousness, putting time with you in first place. Reorder my life, so that I don't hurt people for the sake of tasks, and let Jesus reign in everything. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: List tomorrow's to-dos and reorder them by “God, self, others, tasks”
Tomorrow, read the Bible and pray first, before you pick up your phone
Identify one good thing that is making you anxious, and ask the Lord to show you where it belongs
lessons.noon: “But seek first God’s Kingdom and his righteousness” — Lord, right now I put you back in first place.

lessons.title: Busyness and Fruitfulness
lessons.theme: Fruitfulness depends not on how much we toil but on abiding in the Lord

v: Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.
It is vain for you to rise up early, to stay up late, eating the bread of toil, for he gives sleep to his loved ones.
Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.

lessons.still: Put down what you are doing. Let your shoulders drop and turn your palms upward. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I am not the builder; you are.” Take the task that is making you most anxious today and hand it to the Lord like a brick.
teach: A car with its engine racing but stuck in neutral just roars in place and goes nowhere. Much Christian busyness is like that: high revs, lots of noise, but no forward motion. Busyness is not the same as fruitfulness; real fruitfulness depends on whether we are “in gear” with the Lord.

Psalm 127 says that unless the Lord builds, our labour is “in vain.” This is not a call to laziness but a reminder that if we rise early and stay up late relying on ourselves, all we gain in the end is the bread of toil. Those the Lord loves can sleep in peace, because they know it is God who truly builds.

After a busy night of ministry in Capernaum, Jesus went out to a deserted place to pray the next morning while it was still dark. The disciples said, “Everyone is looking for you,” but he said, “Let's go elsewhere.” His direction was set not by people's needs but by his fellowship with the Father. This week we have been learning to be stewards of time, and it all comes down to this: abide in the Lord first, and then there will be fruit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself — live from the heart and you find joy; live from the head and you find worry. Busyness that relies on ourselves is the self-ruled life at work; rest that relies on the Lord is the self-emptied life letting Christ do the work. Next week we go deeper into the self-emptied life: no longer I, but Christ.
q: Who is God? — “He gives sleep to his loved ones.” What does this show you about how God treats those he loves?
Who am I? — How much of your busyness is “roaring in neutral”?
How shall I respond? — What one task this week will you pray about first before starting work?
lessons.jesus: Jesus had only a little more than three years of public ministry, yet in prayer he could say to the Father, “I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do.” He did not heal every sick person or visit every town, yet he completed everything the Father entrusted to him — that is fruitfulness.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I often use busyness to prove my worth, and effort in place of dependence. Be the builder of my life. I want to be still before you first and then rise to work; not to do the most, but to do what you have entrusted to me, so that all the glory goes to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Get up ten minutes earlier tomorrow and be still before the Lord first
Cancel or postpone one thing that God has not entrusted to you and that you do only to save face
Tonight, give thanks for today's work, and then sleep in peace
lessons.noon: “Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.” — Lord, right now be the builder yourself.

mem.t: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

lessons.title: The Self-Emptied Life Opens onto the Infinite
lessons.theme: Emptying ourselves is not losing ourselves; it is gaining Christ

v: However, I consider those things that were gain to me as a loss for Christ.

Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ
and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us,

lessons.still: Clench both fists and imagine you are gripping the things you care about most: your reputation, your plans, your pride. Slowly open your hands, palms up, and say, “Lord, I let go of what is mine so that I may gain you.” Stay there a moment and feel the lightness of empty hands.
teach: A drop of water that keeps to itself soon evaporates. When it falls into the ocean it seems to “disappear,” but in fact it has become part of the ocean and entered the infinite. Many people fear the self-emptied life, imagining it means erasing their personality and becoming someone with no voice. But the self-emptying the Bible speaks of is a move from the limited self into the limitless Christ.

Paul once had a résumé others envied, yet he said, “for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord.” He was not forced to give things up; he had seen a far greater treasure. Ephesians goes on to say that knowing the love of Christ means being “filled with all the fullness of God.” A heart that has been emptied is exactly the space God fills.

So the self-emptied life is not subtraction but exchange: my limited self for the limitless Christ, my cleverness for his wisdom, my strength for the power that does “exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think.” Change your mindset and you change your life: emptying yourself is not a loss but a gain.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life is not having nothing; it is entering the infinite and living out the infinite. The self-ruled person guards his own drop of water and grows drier the harder he guards it; the self-emptied person lets Jesus reign, all fullness flows from him, and all the glory goes to him.
q: Who is God? — How does a God who does “above all that we ask or think” give you fresh hope about letting go of yourself?
Who am I? — What are you most afraid of losing if you live the self-emptied life?
How shall I respond? — What “gain” are you willing to count as loss for Christ today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus, being in the form of God, emptied himself and became a man. He seemed to lose everything, yet God highly exalted him and gave him the name above every name. Jesus himself proves it: the self-emptied life does not lead into nothingness but into the boundless glory the Father has prepared.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I so often clutch my own little drop of water, afraid of losing it. Today I choose to open my hands and give my limited self to you, the limitless One. Fill me, make knowing you my greatest treasure, and let me live in you a life beyond all I ask or think. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down the three “gains” you find hardest to let go of, and entrust them to the Lord
Whenever you feel the urge to save face today, say quietly, “Christ is my treasure”
Begin memorising this week’s verse: Galatians 2:20
lessons.noon: “the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord” — Lord, right now I let go of myself so that I may gain you.

lessons.title: The Self-Ruled Life Is the Root of the Fall
lessons.theme: Every sin springs from the words “I will”

v: You said in your heart, “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north!
I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!”
For men will be lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,

lessons.still: Quietly count how many times since this morning your heart has said “I want” or “I will.” There is no need to condemn yourself. Simply lay each of those “I will”s honestly before the Lord, one by one, and ask the Holy Spirit to light up the pride hidden in them.
teach: A great tree may have branches and leaves of every shape, but all its nourishment comes up through one taproot. Sin shows itself in many forms too: envy, greed, judging, bitterness, fear. Trace them all the way down and very often you find the same root: the self wants to be in charge. Prune only the leaves and sin keeps growing back; the root has to be dealt with.

Isaiah describes the arrogance of the king of Babylon with five “I will”s in a row: I will ascend into heaven, exalt my throne, sit on the mount of assembly, rise above the clouds, make myself like the Most High. Through the centuries many interpreters have seen in this the shadow of the fallen angel. Either way, the passage lays bare the essence of pride: the creature wants to sit on the Creator’s throne. And when Paul foretells the people of the last days, his list of sins begins right here: “lovers of self.”

In Week 1 we saw the self-ruled life in the Garden of Eden; this week we see how deep its roots go. The good news is that God does not merely prune the leaves; he goes straight for the root. On the cross, the old self that wanted to be king was crucified with Christ. Our response is to recognise that “I will” every day and hand it back to the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our place and grasping power. The self-ruled life is the root of the Fall and the very nature of Satan, which is why only the self-emptied life overcomes Satan. Humility is laying down power and returning to our place: let people be people and let God be God.
q: Who is God? — God alone is the Most High. How does that change the way you see the “I will”s in your heart?
Who am I? — Which sin in your life, traced to its root, is really the self wanting to be in charge?
How shall I respond? — Which “I will” will you turn into “the Lord wills” today?
lessons.jesus: Satan said, “I will ascend into heaven.” Jesus came down from heaven. Satan wanted to exalt his own throne; Jesus washed his disciples’ feet. The direction of heaven is the exact opposite of the direction of hell: one grasps upward, the other pours itself out downward. Jesus chose the downward road.
lessons.pray: Most High God, I confess there are many “I will”s in my heart that want to sit on the throne that belongs only to you. Deal with the root of self-rule in me through the cross. I want to return to my place as a creature, and today in every matter to say: not what I will, but what the Lord wills. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Note three “I will”s today, and beside each write a “the Lord wills” response
Identify a sin that keeps coming back and ask the Lord to show you the root beneath it
Take the first step to yield to someone you have been overbearing with
lessons.noon: “I will make myself like the Most High!” — Lord, right now I don’t want to be king; I want you to be King.

lessons.title: Let Jesus Live in Me
lessons.theme: The old self has died; Christ has become my life

v: For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
When Christ, our life, is revealed, then you will also be revealed with him in glory.
knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.

lessons.still: Close your eyes and quietly say three times, “My life is hidden with Christ in God.” Each time, picture yourself wrapped one layer deeper: in Christ, in God, safe and hidden.
teach: A glove lying on the table can do nothing. But when a hand slides into it, it can write, play the piano, embrace someone. The glove doesn’t have to strain; it only has to let the hand in and let the hand take charge. The Christian life is like that. The point is not how hard I try, but how fully I let Christ live in me.

Paul says, “you died.” That is a finished fact in the past, not a goal we must work to achieve. The old self has already been crucified with Christ, so that we are “no longer in bondage to sin.” Now “Christ, our life” is not just one part of our life or a helper in it; he is life itself.

So the focus of our practice is not “I must be like Christ” but “let Christ live in me.” When someone pushes back at you, instead of gritting your teeth and enduring, pray: “Lord, you are in me; please respond to this person.” That is not passivity; it is handing the glove over to the hand.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life lets Jesus live within. Jesus is my example, and more than that, he is my life. Moving from straining to imitate him to letting him live through me is the move from the self-ruled life of the old self to the self-emptied life of the new self: a defeated life becomes an overcoming life.
q: Who is God? — What kind of security do you feel in being “hidden with Christ in God”?
Who am I? — Do you more often “grit your teeth to imitate” Jesus, or “let him live within you”?
How shall I respond? — In which relationship today will you ask Christ himself to respond?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I can do nothing by myself,” and also, “the Father who lives in me does his works.” That is how Jesus himself lived, letting the Father work fully in him. And now in the same way he lives in us and lives out his life through us.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that my old self has been crucified with you. I will no longer strain in my own strength to be like you; I choose to let you live in me. Today, in my words, my reactions and my decisions, be my life and show your glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: When difficulty comes, pray first: “Lord, please respond through me.”
Write down one situation you have been “gritting your teeth” through, and hand it to the Lord
Meditate on and memorise the first half of Galatians 2:20
lessons.noon: “Christ, our life” — Lord, right now please live in me.

lessons.title: Only the Self-Emptied Can Be Led by the Spirit
lessons.theme: When the flesh insists on being in charge, the Spirit cannot lead

v: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.
For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire.
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.

lessons.still: Imagine you are sitting in the driver’s seat of a car. Quietly get up, move over to the passenger seat, and say to the Lord, “Holy Spirit, please drive.” Stay there a moment, practising truly handing over the wheel.
teach: When two people grip the steering wheel at once, the car will never run straight: one wants to go left, the other right. That is the tug-of-war Galatians describes: “the flesh lusts against the Spirit.” Many believers pray for the Spirit’s guidance while still holding the wheel tight, and then find his leading vague and unclear.

Paul’s answer is not “resist the flesh harder” but “walk by the Spirit.” To “walk” here is to keep in step, one step at a time, like marching behind the one leading the column. He reminds us too that those who belong to Christ “have crucified” the flesh. Since we live by the Spirit, we should also walk by the Spirit: the source of our life and the way we live must match.

The precondition for being led by the Spirit is that the self is willing to step down. When I already have the answer in my heart and only want God to rubber-stamp it, that is self-rule. When I am willing to say, “Lord, even if it’s different from what I think, I’m willing,” that is the self-emptied life. The Holy Spirit never snatches the wheel by force; he waits for us to give up the seat.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. The self-ruled person lives from the head by himself and the more he thinks, the more anxious he becomes; the self-emptied person lives from the heart by the Spirit and receives peace and joy. Only the self-emptied can be led by the Spirit, and only those led by the Spirit can live out Jesus and let Jesus reign.
q: Who is God? — The Holy Spirit is willing to guide your every step. What does that tell you about him?
Who am I? — Do you usually ask God to guide you, or ask him to rubber-stamp your plans?
How shall I respond? — Which decision today will you truly hand over to the Holy Spirit?
lessons.jesus: After his baptism Jesus was “led by the Spirit into the wilderness,” and he returned to Galilee “in the power of the Spirit.” His whole life was a Spirit-led life: when to go, when to stay, whom to speak with, all in obedience to the Father’s leading through the Spirit.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, I confess that I often grip the wheel and only ask you to approve my decisions. Today I give up the driver’s seat and choose to walk by you. Be Lord in my heart; even when your leading is different from what I think, I am willing to follow, so that Jesus may be glorified in me. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Before making a decision, pray first: “Lord, I am willing for you to lead me.”
Write down one matter where you already have the answer and only want God’s stamp of approval
When you notice yourself worrying today, stop and move from the head to the heart in prayer
lessons.noon: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” — Lord, right now I step aside and let you lead.

lessons.title: Only the Self-Emptied Can Be United and Overcome
lessons.theme: Lay down self and we can be of one mind; be of one mind and we overcome

v: make my joy full by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind;
doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;
each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.
They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.

lessons.still: Bring to mind a brother or sister you disagree with. There is no need to work out who is right and who is wrong. Simply pray quietly for them, “Lord, please bless them.” Repeat it three times, and let your own heart soften first.
teach: If everyone in a choir wants their own voice to stand out, all you get is noise. When each singer is willing to listen to the others and adjust, harmony appears. The unity of the church is like that: not everyone being the same, but everyone being willing not to make themselves the centre.

Paul urges the Philippian church to be “like-minded,” and then shows them how: no rivalry, no empty conceit, counting others better than yourself, looking to the interests of others too. The enemy of unity is not differing opinions; it is the self. Revelation pulls back the curtain on the mystery of spiritual warfare: the brothers overcame the accuser by the blood of the Lamb, by the word of their testimony, and because “they didn’t love their life, even to death.” Satan can find no foothold in a self-emptied person.

This week we have moved from the nature of the self-emptied life, to the root of self-rule, to Christ living within, to the Spirit’s guidance, and finally to unity and victory. The self-emptied life is not only a personal discipline; it is the strength of the whole community. Next week we will let the word of God dwell richly in our hearts, because the self-emptied life needs to be fed by the truth.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; humility draws out humility and both sides win. Only the self-emptied can be united, and only the united can overcome. Humility overcomes pride; the self-emptied life overcomes Satan. This is the very foundation for building God’s kingdom system.
q: Who is God? — The blood of the Lamb has already won the victory. How does that shape the way you face spiritual warfare?
Who am I? — How much of the disunity between you and others comes from the self?
How shall I respond? — Toward whom will you deliberately “count others better than yourself” this week?
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper the disciples were still arguing about who was the greatest, but Jesus got up, wrapped a towel around his waist, and bent down to wash their feet. He did not settle the quarrel with argument; he used a self-emptying act that left the proud with nothing to say. Real victory begins with a bent back.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for winning the victory for us through the blood of the Lamb. Remove the rivalry and vanity from my heart; help me count others better than myself and look to their interests too. In my family, my small group and my church, make me a messenger of unity, contending not for myself but only for your kingdom and your glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Pray a specific prayer of blessing for someone you disagree with
In a discussion, affirm the other person’s ideas first before sharing your own
At the weekend, share one experience of the self-emptied life from this week with your spiritual companion
lessons.noon: “each counting others better than himself” — Lord, right now I lay myself down and become one in heart with others.

mem.t: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.

lessons.title: Let the Word Dwell Richly in Your Heart
lessons.theme: God’s word is not a passing visitor; it wants to make its home in your heart

v: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.
I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.

lessons.still: Hold your open Bible against your chest and be still for a moment. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I don’t only want to read your word; I want your word to move into my heart.” Then slowly read this week’s verse aloud, as if you were welcoming a guest through the door.
teach: A guest comes to visit, sits for a while and leaves. Family comes home, puts down their bags, opens the fridge and stays. Many of us read the Bible the way we host a guest: we meet once a day, exchange polite greetings, then close the book and go our separate ways. But Paul says to let the word of Christ “dwell in you richly,” settling in like family, leaving traces of itself everywhere.

“Richly” means not a little, but enough to overflow. And it dwells in the heart, not just the head; it moves into the place where we make decisions and where our feelings arise. The psalmist says, “I have hidden your word in my heart.” To hide it there is to treasure it, and also to prepare: when temptation comes, the heart already holds a word to stand against it.

The eight steps for changing our mindset begin with Information, but they cannot stop there. God’s word must travel from the eyes to the head, from the head to the heart, and finally from the heart into daily life. So this week the focus is not on reading a lot but on letting a few verses settle in deep: meditate on them again and again, memorise them, chew on them through the day.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Scripture is my standard, but a standard must live in the heart before it becomes life. Everything we do flows from the heart. When we receive God’s word with the heart, Information becomes Revelation, and Revelation becomes Conviction, and Jesus reigns in my heart through his word.
q: Who is God? — God is willing to dwell in your heart through his word. What kind of closeness does that make you feel?
Who am I? — Is God’s word in your heart a guest or family?
How shall I respond? — Which verse will you let “move in” to your heart this week?
lessons.jesus: In the depths of his agony on the cross, the words that came from Jesus’ mouth were the words of the Psalms: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” and “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit.” God’s word lived so deeply in his heart that in the darkest hour it flowed out naturally.
lessons.pray: Lord, I often let your word come and go like a hurried guest. Today I open the door of my heart; let your word dwell in me richly. Make it my strength when I meet temptation, my comfort when I am weak, and words of grace when I speak. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write this week’s verse on a card and put it where you will often see it
Quietly recite Colossians 3:16 at three different times today
Before bed, ask yourself: which verse stirred my heart today?
lessons.noon: “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” — Lord, right now let your word speak in my heart.

lessons.title: Four Kinds of Soil
lessons.theme: The same seed, but the harvest depends on the soil of the heart

v: “Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.
Those along the road are those who hear; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their heart, that they may not believe and be saved.
Those on the rock are they who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; but these have no root. They believe for a while, then fall away in time of temptation.
What fell among the thorns, these are those who have heard, and as they go on their way they are choked with cares, riches, and pleasures of life; and they bring no fruit to maturity.
Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance.

lessons.still: Place your hand over your heart and ask the Holy Spirit to walk through the field of your heart like a farmer: “Lord, where in my heart is the hard path? Where are the stones? Where have the thorns grown?” Wait quietly. Don’t argue; let him point them out.
teach: Scatter seed from the same packet onto different ground. On concrete, the birds eat it. In thin soil over rock, it sprouts quickly and withers just as quickly. In ground overgrown with weeds, the seedlings are crowded out and never grow. Only soft, deep, good soil produces full heads of grain. Jesus says the problem is not the seed; the problem is the soil.

Jesus himself explained the four kinds of soil. The heart by the road is hard: the word can’t get in, and the devil snatches it away at once. The heart on the rock is shallow: plenty of enthusiasm but no root, so it falls away when testing comes. The heart among thorns is crowded: the cares, riches and pleasures of this life choke the word. The heart of good soil is honest and good; it holds the word tightly and “produces fruit with perseverance.”

These four soils are not only four kinds of people; often they are four corners of the same person. Today I may be soft about one thing and a hard path about another. The good news is that the soil of the heart can be broken up. Confession is clearing out the stones, simplifying our lives is pulling up the thorns, and holding on with perseverance is letting the roots go deep.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The issue is not whether the preacher is good or whether circumstances are easy, but my own heart. Change your mindset and you change your life. When I let the Lord break up my soil, his word can grow in me from seed to fruit, producing change in my life, my lifestyle and my relationships.
q: Who is God? — God keeps on sowing and never gives up on any patch of ground. What does that show you about him?
Who am I? — Which corner of your heart most needs to be broken up right now?
How shall I respond? — Which stone will you clear out, or which clump of thorns will you pull up?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the sower who doesn’t pick his soil. He sowed the word to Pharisees and to tax collectors and sinners, to the crowds and to one Samaritan woman. His generosity shows us that there is no heart God has given up cultivating.
lessons.pray: Lord of the harvest, thank you that you never stop sowing your word in my heart. Break up the hard paths in me, remove the stones, and pull out the thorns of this life’s worries. I want to be good soil, holding fast to your word and bearing fruit with perseverance, so that you receive the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down the clump of “thorns” that most often crowds out your Bible reading
After reading Scripture today, write down one sentence: “the word I will hold onto”
Delete or pause one distracting app for a day
lessons.noon: “hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance” — Lord, right now make my heart good soil.

lessons.title: Hearing the Word and Doing It
lessons.theme: God’s word is not only a mirror but a road to walk

v: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror;
for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.
But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does.

lessons.still: Recall one thing God said to you the last time you read the Bible. Quietly ask yourself, “Have I done it?” Don’t rush to answer. Let that word act like a mirror and show you what you really look like.
teach: Imagine someone looking in the mirror, seeing a smudge on their face, then turning away and heading out to meet people as they are. How absurd! James says that is what hearing without doing is like: we are moved in a service, enlightened while reading Scripture, and then we close the Bible and “immediately forget,” carrying on just as we were.

James calls this “deluding your own selves”: we hear a lot, so we think we are spiritual; we know a lot, so we think we have already done it. He calls God’s word “the perfect law of freedom,” not rules that bind us but truth that sets us free. The keys to blessing are three: look closely, keep at it, and actually do it.

In the eight steps for changing our mindset, Information, Revelation and Conviction are followed straight away by Practice. Conviction without practice is just a feeling. Only with practice can there be Review, Correction and Repetition, and finally Multiplication. You don’t need to do ten things today; just take one thing God has said to you and do it once, today.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Change your mindset and you change your life; change your life and you change your lifestyle. Hearing the word shapes the mindset; doing the word shapes the way we live. Hearing without doing leaves the mindset stuck in the head. When we receive with the heart and practise by the Spirit, God’s word becomes my life and Jesus reigns in my everyday living.
q: Who is God? — God calls his word “the law of freedom.” Does that change the way you see his commands?
Who am I? — Which recent word from God did you hear and then “immediately forget”?
How shall I respond? — Which word will you actually “do” today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said that whoever hears his words and does them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock. That is exactly how he lived. The love for enemies he taught, he did on the cross; the self-denial he spoke of, he lived out his whole life. With Jesus, word and life were never separated.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess I often hear and forget, letting being moved stay just a feeling. Forgive me for deceiving myself. Today I want to look closely into your word and actually do it. Holy Spirit, remind me and strengthen me, so that I may be blessed in what I do and bring you glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Pick one sentence from a recent Bible reading or sermon and do it today
In the evening, review: Did I do it? What needs correcting?
Tell a spiritual companion about your experience of doing the word today
lessons.noon: “be doers of the word, and not only hearers” — Lord, right now help me put your word into practice.

lessons.title: The Sword of the Spirit
lessons.theme: God’s word first cuts me open, then fights for me

v: And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God;

For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

lessons.still: Sit quietly and picture yourself as a patient lying on an operating table. Say to the Lord, “Lord, let your word open me up and discern even the thoughts and intentions of my heart.” Hand over to him one corner of your life you would rather he didn’t touch.
teach: A surgeon’s scalpel is very sharp, but it cuts in order to heal. God’s word is also a sword, and a two-edged one: one edge faces outward to resist the enemy in spiritual warfare; the other faces inward, piercing our hearts and exposing hidden motives. Many people want only to swing the sword at the enemy, but are unwilling to let it operate on themselves first.

Of all the pieces of armour in Ephesians, only one is a weapon of attack: the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Notice it is the Spirit’s sword. It is not us using verses to crush people, but the Holy Spirit wielding God’s word. Hebrews says this word is “living and active” and able to discern “the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” We do not only read God’s word; it reads us.

In Week 19 we saw Jesus overcome temptation with “It is written.” Today we go one step deeper: the sword must first cut open my heart and remove the self-ruled motives; only then can I hold it steady in battle. Those who have been opened up by God’s word are the ones who can overcome by it.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life overcomes Satan. God’s word first deals with the self in me and brings me back to my place; the enemy finds no foothold in a person whom the truth has opened up and humbled. The one wielding the sword is not my cleverness but the Spirit’s guidance, and the glory of victory goes to Jesus.
q: Who is God? — God’s word is “living and active.” What does that tell you about the God who speaks it?
Who am I? — Do you more often use God’s word to deal with others, or let it deal with you first?
How shall I respond? — Which “intention” of your heart needs to be discerned by God’s word?
lessons.jesus: Three times in the wilderness Jesus resisted the devil with “It is written,” and every stroke struck home. Yet he also let the same Scriptures govern his own path, willingly letting what was written about his suffering be fulfilled in him. He obeyed God’s word all the way to the cross, and then, holding that sword, won the complete victory.
lessons.pray: Lord, your word is sharper than any two-edged sword. I want to let it open me up first and expose the pride and self-will hidden in my heart. Heal me and cleanse me, then teach me to take up this sword under the Spirit’s guidance and stand firm in temptation and battle. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Memorise a verse you most often need for facing temptation
As you read Scripture today, ask: “Where is this passage cutting me open?”
Take back something you once said when you used Scripture to accuse someone
lessons.noon: “the word of God is living and active” — Lord, right now let your word open me up and also protect me.

lessons.title: Teaching One Another with God’s Word
lessons.theme: The word that dwells in the heart must flow out through our relationships

v: Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness,
that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.
These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart;
and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

lessons.still: Quietly think of someone near you: a family member, someone in your group, a colleague. Ask the Lord for them: “Lord, give me a word of blessing from your Scripture that I can give to them.” Wait, and let a verse rise to mind.
teach: A well that only takes water in and never lets it out turns stagnant; a river with a source and an outlet stays clear and flowing. God’s word does not dwell in our hearts to turn us into reservoirs of knowledge, but to flow through us to others. The second half of Colossians 3:16 says exactly this: “teaching and admonishing one another.”

Paul says Scripture is “profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness,” so that God’s people may be “thoroughly equipped for every good work.” Deuteronomy paints an everyday picture: talking about God’s words at home, on the road, when lying down and when getting up. Teaching doesn’t only happen from the pulpit; it happens even more around the dinner table and along the way.

This week we have let God’s word dwell in our hearts, broken up the soil, put the word into practice and let it cut us open, and now we let it flow outward. Next week we will learn another way of flowing out: the ministry of intercession. Let God’s word and prayer become the two hands with which we serve others.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. God’s word first becomes life in my heart, then we teach one another in our relationships, and only then can it multiply and build God’s kingdom system. With psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, speaking the truth in love, humility draws out humility and we are built up together.
q: Who is God? — God tells his people to talk about his words in everyday life. What does that show you about how much he values family and relationships?
Who am I? — Are you a well that only takes in, or a flowing river?
How shall I respond? — Which verse will you give to which person this week?
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus walked with the two disciples on the road to Emmaus and, “beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.” He taught them on the road until their hearts burned within them. This is exactly what it means to teach one another with God’s word in everyday life.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for letting your word dwell in my heart this week. Don’t let it stop in me; let it flow through me to my family and my brothers and sisters. Teach me to speak the truth in love and to encourage others with Scripture, not to show myself off but so that people are built up and you are glorified. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Pass a verse on to someone who needs encouragement
Today, at the table or on the road, talk with your family about one word from God
Share this week’s memory verse in your small group or with your spiritual companion
lessons.noon: “These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart” — Lord, right now let your word flow from my mouth as blessing.

mem.t: I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men,

lessons.title: Abraham’s Intercession
lessons.theme: Intercession is standing within God’s heart and pleading with him for others

v: Abraham came near, and said, “Will you consume the righteous with the wicked?
What if there are fifty righteous within the city? Will you consume and not spare the place for the fifty righteous who are in it?
