May it be far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”

lessons.still: Quietly picture yourself, like Abraham, “coming near” into God’s presence. Bring no needs of your own, only one person’s name. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I have come before you for them.”
teach: A child runs to his father and says, “Dad, my little brother knows he was wrong. Could you give him one more chance?” The child dares to say this because he knows his father’s heart. It was the same when Abraham interceded for Sodom: God first told him what he was about to do, and Abraham “came near” and pleaded with God for the city.

Abraham’s intercession has three marks. He “came near”: intercession is an act of drawing close to God. He pleaded on the basis of God’s character: “Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?” And he was humble yet persistent, going down from fifty to ten, each time setting himself aside and asking once more. Sodom was destroyed in the end, yet God “remembered Abraham” and brought Lot out.

Intercession is not persuading a reluctant God; it is stepping into God’s heart and working together with him. The more Abraham interceded, the better he came to know God’s justice and mercy. It is the same for us: intercession is God inviting us to stand beside him and care for this world together with him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Intercession is praying for others, not for ourselves; it is the prayer of the self-emptied life. The focus is not on my own needs but on God’s heart and the salvation of others. Interceding humbly and persistently is letting Jesus reign in our prayers and taking part in building God’s kingdom system.
q: Who is God? — God told Abraham what he was about to do. What does that show you about how he regards those who intercede?
Who am I? — In your prayers, how does what you ask for yourself compare with what you ask for others?
How shall I respond? — For which “city” — your family, your workplace, your neighbourhood — will you come near and intercede?
lessons.jesus: Abraham interceded for Sodom down to ten righteous people; Jesus went further. He himself became the Righteous One who died in the place of sinners. He did not only intercede for the city; he personally bore the judgment the city deserved.
lessons.pray: Judge of all the earth, you are just and full of mercy. Teach me to come near like Abraham and intercede for my family, my colleagues and this city. I come before you not on my own merits but in the name of Jesus; have mercy, and let the lost be saved. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down the names of three people or places you will keep praying for
Today, pray specifically for five minutes for a friend or relative who does not yet believe
Start an “intercession log” page in your prayer journal
lessons.noon: “Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?” — Lord, right now I ask your mercy on the city where I live.

lessons.title: Standing in the Gap
lessons.theme: An intercessor is the person God looks for at the breach

v: Moses returned to the LORD, and said, “Oh, this people have sinned a great sin, and have made themselves gods of gold.
Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin— and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”
“I sought for a man among them who would build up the wall and stand in the gap before me for the land, that I would not destroy it; but I found no one.

lessons.still: Quietly stand up, or picture yourself standing before a gap in a wall. Say to the Lord, “Lord, you are looking for someone. Here I am.” Then ask him to show you where there is a breach around you.
teach: When a crack appears in a levee and no one plugs it, the flood will sweep away the whole village. City walls in ancient times were the same: a single breach was where the enemy would break in. In Ezekiel God says, “I sought for a man among them who would… stand in the gap.” God was looking for an intercessor, but “found no one.”

Moses was one who stood in the gap. The people worshipped the golden calf and committed a great sin. Moses did not make excuses for them; he admitted, “this people have sinned a great sin.” But then he said, “Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book.” He placed himself between the people and judgment, preferring to be blotted out himself rather than see the people destroyed.

Standing in the gap is not pointing out other people’s faults; it is carrying their burdens. When we see breaches in our families, churches and society, our first reaction is often to criticise and complain. But God invites us not just to stand outside the wall pointing fingers, but to step into the breach and shield them in prayer.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The focus is not on other people’s faults, but on whether I will stand before God for them. Criticism is self-rule, standing on high ground to judge; intercession is self-emptying, stepping into the breach to carry the load. Humility draws out humility; those who stand in the gap are repairing the walls for God’s kingdom system.
q: Who is God? — God “sought for a man.” What does that show you about how unwilling he is for people to perish?
Who am I? — Faced with the breaches around you, do you more often criticise or intercede?
How shall I respond? — For which breach will you stand before God every day this week?
lessons.jesus: Moses said, “blot me out,” but God did not grant it. Jesus, though, truly was forsaken by the Father, so that our names could be written in the book of life. He is the ultimate one who stood in the gap, closing with his own body the rift between God’s judgment and human sin.
lessons.pray: Lord, you are looking for someone to stand in the gap, and I want to say: here I am. Forgive me for so often criticising and so seldom interceding. Today I stand before you for my family, my church and my nation; have mercy, bring revival, and repair every broken wall. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Turn a person or group you often criticise into someone you pray for
Pray for ten minutes about the biggest breach in your family right now
Agree with a spiritual companion to pray together about one matter this week
lessons.noon: “I sought for a man among them who would build up the wall” — Lord, right now I am willing to stand in the gap for others.

lessons.title: Jesus Intercedes for Us
lessons.theme: Our intercession rests on Jesus’ unceasing intercession

v: “Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word,
that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.
Therefore he is also able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, seeing that he lives forever to make intercession for them.

lessons.still: Listen quietly: right now, at this very moment, Jesus is at the Father’s right hand praying for you. You don’t need to say anything; just receive this fact. Let the words “he is praying for me” sink slowly to the bottom of your heart.
teach: Waking in the night as a child and hearing your parents in the next room softly praying for you is a sense of safety you remember for life. John 17 lets us “overhear” Jesus’ prayer. On the night he was betrayed, he prayed not only for the disciples in front of him but also “for those also who will believe in me through their word.” You and I are in that prayer.

Jesus’ intercession has clear content: keep them from the evil one, sanctify them by the truth, make them one, so that the world may believe. Hebrews goes further: he “lives forever to make intercession for them.” Jesus’ intercession did not end at the cross. Today he is still interceding for us before the Father, and that is why he is able to “save to the uttermost.”

This changes the foundation of our intercession. We are not lonely prayer warriors; we are joining a prayer that has long been under way. When I intercede for others, I am following the heart of Jesus our High Priest. And this lets us rest: even when my prayers are weak, his intercession never stops.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example, even in intercession, where I follow him. His prayer for the disciples’ unity is the very heart of building God’s kingdom system. Our intercession does not depend on our own zeal or how long we pray, but on Jesus’ name and his intercession, so all the glory goes to him.
q: Who is God? — Jesus “lives forever to make intercession.” What does that tell you about his love for you?
Who am I? — Knowing that Jesus is praying for you, what burden can you lay down today?
How shall I respond? — Following Jesus’ heart, which brothers and sisters will you pray for to be one?
lessons.jesus: Before Peter denied him three times, Jesus told him, “I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.” Jesus’ intercession held Peter up not only while he stood but even more when he fell, and it prepared a calling for him once he turned back.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you that right now you are praying for me before the Father. When I am weak, when I fall, even when I forget to pray, your intercession never stops. Bring my prayers into step with your heart, so that I pray for my brothers and sisters to be kept, made holy and made one, and the world may believe in you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Read John 17 and circle what Jesus asks for his disciples
Using the content of Jesus’ prayer, intercede for each member of your small group
Pray for a brother or sister who is stumbling, and send them a word of encouragement
lessons.noon: “he lives forever to make intercession for them” — Lord, right now thank you for interceding for me.

lessons.title: Praying for Those in Authority
lessons.theme: Our intercession must stretch wide enough to include all people and all in authority

v: I exhort therefore, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and givings of thanks be made for all men,
for kings and all who are in high places, that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence.
For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior,
who desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth.
Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the LORD for it; for in its peace you will have peace.”

lessons.still: Quietly imagine looking down from a height on the city where you live: its streets, schools, hospitals, government offices. Say to the Lord, “Lord, this city is yours; please give it peace.” Then bring to mind the name of one person in authority.
teach: If the passengers on a ship do nothing but complain about the captain and no one prays for him, the complaining won’t make the ship any safer. When Paul wrote, the power in charge was the Roman Empire, which often persecuted Christians, yet he said, “first of all” pray for “all men,” “for kings and all who are in high places.” This is not a political position; it is a heavenly perspective.

Paul says the purpose of this intercession is “that we may lead a tranquil and quiet life in all godliness and reverence,” and the deeper reason is that God “desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth.” Jeremiah, too, told the exiles in Babylon to seek the peace of the very city that had destroyed their homes. God’s people are not bystanders in society; they are watchmen in prayer.

Praying for those in authority does not mean approving of everything they do; it means acknowledging that ultimate authority is in God’s hands. Shift your perspective from “they decide my situation” to “God holds their hearts.” Then we need not be cynical, nor simply drift with the current; instead we keep watch over the land in prayer.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The kingdom, the power and the glory all belong to God. Praying for those in authority is praying the Lord’s Prayer: “Your kingdom come. Your will be done on earth.” Our focus is on Jesus, not on our circumstances; letting Jesus reign over our nation and our city is our true hope.
q: Who is God? — God “desires all people to be saved.” What does that show you about how wide his heart is?
Who am I? — Toward those in authority over you, do you more often complain or intercede?
How shall I respond? — Which person in authority (in government, at work, at school) will you pray for specifically?
lessons.jesus: Standing before Pilate, Jesus said, “You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above.” He saw clearly the true sovereignty behind earthly power. He did not curse those who sentenced him to death; instead, on the cross he prayed for them: “Father, forgive them.”
lessons.pray: King of kings, I pray for the leaders of my nation, the officials of my city, the managers at my workplace, and the teachers in our schools. Give them wisdom and justice, so that we may live godly, upright and peaceful lives. Above all, let all people be saved and come to know the truth; may your kingdom come to this land. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Pray once for your nation’s leader and once for the head of your city
Ask for one specific blessing for your direct manager or your teacher
When you watch the news, turn one piece of bad news into a prayer
lessons.noon: “Seek the peace of the city” — Lord, right now I ask for peace for my city and its leaders.

lessons.title: Intercession Changes the Intercessor
lessons.theme: As I pray for others, God is changing me

v: The LORD restored Job’s prosperity when he prayed for his friends. The LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before.
Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.

lessons.still: Think of someone who once hurt or misunderstood you. Be still for a moment. You don’t need to force any feeling; simply tell the Lord honestly, “Lord, I choose to pray for them.” Then say their name and ask the Lord to bless them.
teach: It has been said that it is hard to pray sincerely for someone while continuing to hate them. Intercession is like a window: we open it so that God’s light can shine into someone else’s life, only to discover that the first person lit up is the one standing at the window.

Job’s three friends wounded him with bad theology, yet God told them to ask Job to pray for them. The text says, “Yahweh restored Job’s prosperity when he prayed for his friends.” The turning point did not come when Job prayed for himself, but when he interceded for those who had hurt him. James also says, “pray for one another, that you may be healed.” Intercession is healing that flows both ways.

This week we have gone from Abraham, to Moses, to Jesus, to praying for all people, and now we come back to ourselves. As intercessors stand in the gap for others, their own hearts are enlarged, healed and changed into the likeness of Jesus. Next week we will learn to discern the Holy Spirit’s guidance, and prayer is exactly where we hear his voice.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Praying for those who have hurt me is the deepest practice of the self-emptied life. Pride provokes pride and both sides lose; intercession draws out humility and both sides win. When I intercede for my “2,” God produces the fruit of the Spirit in me, and the relationship is renewed as well.
q: Who is God? — God restored Job as he prayed for his friends. What does that show you about how God heals people?
Who am I? — Who is the hardest person for you to pray for?
How shall I respond? — Are you willing to pray for that person once a day this week?
lessons.jesus: Jesus taught, “love your enemies… and pray for those who… persecute you,” and he lived it himself. As the nails went through his hands and feet, he said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” Intercession kept him living in love even in the deepest wound.
lessons.pray: Lord, you tell me to pray for those who persecute me. I admit this is hard, but I choose to obey. Today I bless those who have hurt me; please heal the pain and bitterness in my heart too. Change me as I intercede, so that I become more and more like Jesus, who prayed for others on the cross. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Ask for one specific blessing for someone who has hurt you
Share a need with a spiritual companion and pray for each other
Write down what God has changed in your heart through intercession this week
lessons.noon: “when he prayed for his friends” — Lord, right now I pray to you for the person who is hard for me to love.

mem.t: For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.

lessons.title: Children Led by the Spirit
lessons.theme: The Spirit’s guidance flows from the relationship between a child and the Father

v: For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.
For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”
The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God;

lessons.still: Quietly call out in the simplest way: “Abba, Father.” Slowly repeat it a few times, like a child calling for his father in the dark. Let the Holy Spirit bear witness in your heart that you are God’s beloved child.
teach: A child lost in a strange city doesn’t need to worry about the map if his father is holding his hand. A hired guide, on the other hand, must constantly worry about making a mistake and having his pay docked. Many believers treat “seeking God’s guidance” like an exam: afraid of choosing wrong, afraid God will be displeased, afraid of missing his “perfect will.” Paul says that is the heart of a slave, not the heart of a child.

Romans 8 links being “led by the Spirit of God” with being “children of God.” Guidance is not an occasional special experience; it is a mark of our identity as children. What the Spirit brings us is not a return “to fear” but the intimacy of being able to cry “Abba! Father!” He also “testifies with our spirit.” Guidance starts with relationship, not with technique.

Change your mindset and you change your life. Discerning God’s will begins not with asking “What must I do so I don’t get it wrong?” but “How is my relationship with my Father?” A child who often rests in the Father’s arms naturally grows more and more familiar with his voice. This week we are learning discernment and obedience, but all of it must flow from this security of being his children.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. The self-ruled person gropes along by himself, living from the head and growing anxious; the self-emptied person leans on the Father like a child, living from the heart and finding joy. Being led by the Spirit is not a mysterious experience but the everyday life of children who walk with the Father and let Jesus reign.
q: Who is God? — The Holy Spirit enables you to cry “Abba! Father!” What does that tell you about God?
Who am I? — When you seek God’s guidance, are you more like a child or like a fearful slave?
How shall I respond? — How will you draw near to the Father as his child today?
lessons.jesus: In the depths of his anguish in Gethsemane, Jesus still cried out, “Abba, Father.” His obedience did not come from fear but from love and trust. Jesus is the firstborn Son led by the Spirit; his whole life was a Son walking with his Father.
lessons.pray: Abba Father, thank you for making me your child through the Holy Spirit. I confess I often come seeking your will with a slave’s fear. Today I want to put my hand in yours like a child. Holy Spirit, lead my every step, so that I may follow at peace in your love. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Three times today, quietly call out in your heart: “Abba, Father.”
Write down one decision you are afraid of getting wrong, and entrust it to your heavenly Father
Begin memorising this week’s verse: Romans 8:14
lessons.noon: “as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God” — Lord, right now I follow you as your child.

lessons.title: Discerning God’s Will
lessons.theme: Only a renewed mind can discern the will of God

v: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.
Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.
Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding.
In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.

lessons.still: Sit up straight with your hands on your knees and quietly offer yourself: “Lord, my eyes, my mouth, my hands and my feet, I give them all to you.” As you speak, hand over each part in your heart.
teach: If a radio is tuned to the wrong frequency, you hear only static, even though the station is broadcasting all the time. Seeking God’s will is like that. Often the problem is not that God isn’t speaking, but that this world has pulled our “frequency” off station. Paul says we must first “be transformed by the renewing of your mind,” and then we can “prove” God’s will.

The order in Romans 12 matters. First, “present your bodies”; then, “don’t be conformed to this world”; and only then, “prove.” Offering ourselves is the posture of the self-emptied life, renewal is a change of mindset, and proving is testing and confirming in everyday life. Proverbs adds the other side: “don’t lean on your own understanding,” but “in all your ways acknowledge him.”

The biggest principles for discerning God’s will are already written in the Bible: Scripture is my standard. The Spirit’s guidance never contradicts Scripture. In matters the Bible does not spell out, we come with a heart already offered and a renewed mindset; we acknowledge him, pray, listen to the counsel of spiritual companions, and then discern step by step.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Here the three foundations come together: Jesus is my example; Scripture is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide. Shift your perspective from the human, the earthly and the temporary to the divine, the heavenly and the eternal. With a renewed mind we can discern the good, well-pleasing and perfect will of God.
q: Who is God? — God’s will is “good, well-pleasing, and perfect.” Does that change how you feel about his will?
Who am I? — What in this world most often pulls your “frequency” off station?
How shall I respond? — What decision are you facing that needs you to offer yourself first and then discern?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, and to accomplish his work.” He often withdrew to lonely places to pray, tuning his heart before the Father. He discerned God’s will not by the applause of the crowds nor by Satan’s shortcuts, but through unbroken fellowship with the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord, I want to present my body as a living sacrifice. Renew my mind so that I am no longer conformed to this world. I will not lean on my own understanding; in all my ways I acknowledge you. Make my paths straight, and help me discern and delight in your good, well-pleasing and perfect will. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Hold a decision you are weighing up against a relevant passage of Scripture
Ask a mature spiritual companion for counsel about this decision
Take in one fewer voice from the world today, and keep five extra minutes of silence
lessons.noon: “In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” — Lord, right now I acknowledge you.

lessons.title: Forbidden by the Holy Spirit
lessons.theme: A closed door is also the Spirit’s guidance

v: When they had gone through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.
When they had come opposite Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit didn’t allow them.
A vision appeared to Paul in the night. There was a man of Macedonia standing, begging him and saying, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.”
When he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that the Lord had called us to preach the Good News to them.

lessons.still: Recall a door that has recently closed in front of you: a plan, an opportunity, a hope. Quietly lay it before the Lord and say, “Lord, I don’t understand, but I believe you are leading.”
teach: A satnav will sometimes say, “Road closed ahead. Recalculating route.” We rarely thank it for that, yet it often steers us away from dangers we can’t see. On his second missionary journey Paul ran into two “road closures”: the Holy Spirit forbade them to speak the word in Asia, and the Spirit of Jesus would not allow them to go into Bithynia.

The places Paul wanted to go were all good places, and preaching the gospel there was a good thing. But the Holy Spirit closed two doors, and only at Troas did he open the door to Macedonia through a vision. As a result, the gospel entered Europe for the first time and the church in Philippi was born. Notice that Paul did not stop and wait for a vision; he was redirected as he kept walking. And “concluding that the Lord had called us” shows they discerned and confirmed it together.

Being forbidden by the Spirit often tests our self-emptied life more than having a door opened. When the self-ruled person meets a closed door, they push, ram and complain; the self-emptied person stops and says, “Lord, where do you want to take me?” A closed door is not failure; it is God recalculating the route.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Letting Jesus reign includes giving him the authority to say “no.” The self-ruled accept only open doors; the self-emptied also submit to closed ones. Our focus is on Jesus, not on whether circumstances go our way. Both the Spirit’s closing and his opening serve to build God’s kingdom system and carry the gospel further.
q: Who is God? — God sometimes guides by saying “no.” What does that tell you about his wisdom?
Who am I? — When you face a closed door, do you usually push, ram, or stop and ask?
How shall I respond? — How will you look afresh at the door that recently closed?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus heard that Lazarus was ill, he did not set off at once; he stayed two more days. The disciples didn’t understand, and neither did Martha and Mary. But Jesus submitted to the Father’s timing, and the result was not one sick man healed but a man four days dead raised to life, and God received far greater glory.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess I often complain about closed doors and even try to force them open in my own strength. Today I hand this door to you, trusting that your “no” is also love. Holy Spirit, lead me; keep me from losing heart as I wait, and when a new direction opens, let me follow at once. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write one sentence of thanks for a door that has recently closed
Recall a time when a “closed door” later turned out to be a blessing
Pray with a spiritual companion to discern a matter that feels stuck
lessons.noon: “they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit” — Lord, right now I submit to your “no” and wait for you to open the way.

lessons.title: Let Peace Rule
lessons.theme: Let the peace of Christ be the referee in your heart

v: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.
In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Take three slow, deep breaths. Name each worry in your heart one by one and hand it to God, then thank him for one thing. Quietly notice: after entrusting them to him, does your heart feel tighter or looser?
teach: When two teams are arguing heatedly on the field, who has the final say? The referee’s whistle. Paul says, “let the peace … rule in your hearts,” and the word “rule” in the original carries the sense of acting as referee or arbiter. When several voices are arguing in your heart, let the peace of Christ blow the whistle and decide.

This peace is not a feeling produced by smooth circumstances; it is “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding,” which God himself uses to “guard” our hearts and minds after prayer, petition and thanksgiving. Paul also links this peace with being “called in one body.” The Spirit’s guidance rarely tears people away from the body; it leads them into unity in love.

But be careful: peace is not the same as comfort. When Jonah ran away towards Tarshish, he slept soundly in the hold of the ship. That was not God’s peace but numbness. True peace often comes after obedience; even when the road ahead is hard, the heart is clear and settled. So in discerning guidance, peace is one of the referees, but it blows the whistle together with Scripture, prayer, and the confirmation of spiritual companions.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart by the Spirit and you find joy; live from the head by yourself and you find worry. Letting Christ’s peace rule is letting Jesus reign in my heart. The self-ruled person is dragged along by worries; the self-emptied person hands worries to God with a thankful heart, and peace becomes the arbiter within.
q: Who is God? — God’s peace “surpasses all understanding.” What does that tell you about him?
Who am I? — Which voices are arguing in your heart right now?
How shall I respond? — Which worry will you entrust to God, letting the peace of Christ blow the whistle?
lessons.jesus: The disciples panicked in the storm, but Jesus was asleep in the stern on a cushion. He woke and said, “Peace! Be still!” and the wind ceased. Jesus also told his disciples, “Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you.” His peace did not come from the absence of storms but from being with the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I hand all the worries in my heart to you. Thank you for giving me peace that surpasses understanding. Let your peace rule in my heart and blow the whistle for me as I discern and decide. And keep me from mistaking numbness for peace; let me experience your real presence through obedience. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down today’s biggest worry, pray about it, then cross it out
Before making a decision, pause for three minutes and notice whether your heart is at peace
Before bed, list three things you are thankful for and go to sleep in peace
lessons.noon: “let the peace of God rule in your hearts” — Lord, right now let your peace rule in me.

lessons.title: Obey Without Delay
lessons.theme: Hear it and do it; delayed obedience is disobedience

v: I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.
The Spirit said to Philip, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot.”
Philip ran to him, and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, “Do you understand what you are reading?”

lessons.still: Quietly ask the Lord, “Lord, is there something you told me long ago that I still haven’t done?” Wait until it comes clearly to mind. Then say to the Lord, “I will do it today.”
teach: The weather forecast on the radio says, “Thunderstorms this afternoon.” You hear it, you agree, but you don’t take an umbrella, and you get soaked just the same. Knowing without acting at once is the same as not knowing. This week we have been learning to discern the Spirit’s guidance, and the final lesson is the most crucial step: when you hear, go and do it.

Philip had just led a great revival in Samaria, yet an angel told him to go to a desert road. He got up and went. Then the Spirit said, “Go near, and join yourself to this chariot,” and the text says Philip “ran.” Because he obeyed at once, he arrived just in time to hear the eunuch reading Isaiah, and so the gospel reached Africa. The psalmist says, “I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.”

Often it is not that we can’t hear the Spirit, but that we hear and then bargain: when I’m ready, when the time is right, when someone else goes first. Delay is another form of self-rule: I still want to decide when I will obey. Next week we will learn to take up the cross, and obeying at once is the first step in denying ourselves daily.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The path of service runs Spirit, Insight, Life, Service, God: first led by the Holy Spirit, then understanding the truth, living out the life of Jesus, serving in his authority, and finally giving the glory to God. Obeying without delay is letting Jesus reign; delayed obedience means the self is still sitting on the throne.
q: Who is God? — The Holy Spirit spoke to Philip so specifically. What does that tell you about his guidance?
Who am I? — What has God already told you that you are still putting off?
How shall I respond? — What will you “run” to do today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus called the fishermen, “Come after me,” and immediately they left their nets and followed him. And Jesus himself lived this way even more: from the wilderness to the cross he said, “I have come to do your will,” and never bargained with the Father. His obedience was immediate, complete, and all the way to the end.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, I confess I often hear your voice and then delay and make excuses. Today I will stop bargaining. Give me Philip’s running feet, so that when I hear, I go and do. May my obedience never be delayed, so that Jesus reigns in my life and receives all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Finish today one thing God reminded you of long ago that you keep putting off
Today, when you feel prompted to care for someone, act within five minutes
At the weekend, share with your spiritual companion one time you obeyed without delay this week
lessons.noon: “I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.” — Lord, right now I want to obey you at once.

mem.t: He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.

lessons.title: The Cross Taken Up Willingly
lessons.theme: The cross is not something forced on us but a willing laying down of self

v: Therefore the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, that I may take it again.
No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father.”
He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.”

lessons.still: Quietly kneel, or bow down before the Lord in your heart. Slowly say Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane: “Not what I desire, but what you desire.” As you say it, think of the one thing you least want to hand over right now.
teach: Illness and giving blood both involve losing blood, but their meaning is completely different: one is something that happens to us against our will, the other a willing gift. Many people take “bearing the cross” to mean putting up with everything unpleasant: traffic jams, illness, a difficult colleague are all called “my cross.” But the cross Jesus spoke of is not suffering forced upon us; it is self-denial freely chosen out of love.

Jesus said, “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.” He was not a victim defeated by Roman soldiers but the Good Shepherd who laid down his life of his own accord. Yet this willingness was not easy. In Gethsemane he fell on his face and honestly said, “let this cup pass away from me,” and then, “nevertheless, not what I desire.” Denying ourselves does not mean there is no struggle; it means choosing the Father’s will in the midst of the struggle.

So the key word in bearing the cross is “willingly.” Change your mindset: stop asking, “Why is this happening to me?” and start asking, “Lord, in this situation, what do you want me to lay down for love’s sake?” Suffering in itself does not make us holy; willing self-denial does.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Denying ourselves means living for Jesus and for others, not for ourselves. The self-ruled person who suffers against his will grows bitter; the self-emptied person who lays himself down willingly finds freedom. Jesus is my example: he had power to lay his life down and power to take it again. As we follow him, we move from victims to overcomers.
q: Who is God? — Jesus laid down his life “by myself.” What does that tell you about his love?
Who am I? — How much of what you call your “cross” is simply something that happened to you?
How shall I respond? — In what matter today will you “willingly” lay down your own way?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was arrested, Peter drew his sword to defend him, but Jesus said, “Or do you think that I couldn’t ask my Father, and he would even now send me more than twelve legions of angels?” He had the power to get away, yet he chose to stay. Jesus on the cross was not powerless; he was willingly laying himself down.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for laying down your life for me willingly, not under compulsion but out of love. I confess I often call every inconvenience a cross, yet seldom deny myself willingly. Today I pray your prayer: not what I desire, but what you desire. Give me a willing and glad heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Tell apart one thing that has simply “happened to you” and one thing where you can willingly deny yourself
In some small matter, deliberately set aside your own way so that someone else’s can go ahead
Begin memorising this week’s verse: Luke 9:23
lessons.noon: “not what I desire, but what you desire” — Lord, right now I willingly hand over my own way.

lessons.title: A Grain of Wheat
lessons.theme: Only by dying can it bear much fruit

v: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life.
If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there my servant will also be. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.

lessons.still: Hold a grain of rice or a seed in your palm (or imagine one). Look at it quietly and ask the Lord, “Lord, which part of my life needs to fall into the ground?” Then open your hand and let it drop.
teach: A grain of wheat kept in a beautiful box can last for years, but it will only ever be one grain. When the farmer buries it in the soil, its husk splits and rots and it looks finished; yet before long a stalk springs up and bears dozens, even hundreds of grains. Only by losing its own shape can it become many.

When Jesus said this, some Greeks had come asking to see him, which looked like a fine moment for his fame to spread. But Jesus said, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified,” and then he spoke of death. His glory was not to be admired by more people but to fall into the ground and die like a grain of wheat and bear much fruit. The cross brought salvation to every nation and people.

“Hating your life” is not self-loathing; it means no longer treating your own life as the highest value. If we hoard our time, gifts and reputation, they will remain a single grain. If we let them fall into the ground for the Lord and for others, they will bear much fruit. The end of self-denial is not disappearing; it is multiplying.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life is not having nothing; it is entering the infinite and living out the infinite, just as one grain becomes many. The last of the eight steps for changing our mindset is Multiplication. Only a life willing to fall into the ground can build God’s kingdom system and let Jesus receive all the glory.
q: Who is God? — God brings “much fruit” out of death. What does that show you about how he works?
Who am I? — What in your life is like a grain of wheat kept in a box, tightly hoarded?
How shall I respond? — Which gift or portion of time will you “bury” in someone else’s life?
lessons.jesus: Jesus himself is that grain of wheat. He was buried in the tomb and rose again on the third day. On the day of Pentecost three thousand people came to the Lord, and the gospel spread from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. Every person who believes in him today is fruit from that one grain.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the grain of wheat that fell into the ground and died, and I am fruit you have borne. Keep me from hoarding my own life. I give you my time, my gifts and my reputation; let them fall into the ground and bear fruit in others’ lives, so that the Father is glorified. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Spend time accompanying or teaching a believer younger than you
Take one gift you have been holding back and use it to serve the church this week
Write down an experience where something in you “died” and God then made it bear fruit
lessons.noon: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone” — Lord, right now I am willing to fall into the ground.

lessons.title: Carried Daily
lessons.theme: Self-denial is not one heroic act but a choice made every day

v: always carrying in the body the putting to death of the Lord Jesus, that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body.
For we who live are always delivered to death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus may be revealed in our mortal flesh.
Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward person is decaying, yet our inward person is renewed day by day.

lessons.still: Think back over the day since you got up: was there a small moment when you could have chosen to give way but didn’t? Don’t condemn yourself; simply tell the Lord quietly, “Lord, in the moments ahead, I want to take up my cross daily.”
teach: Many of us imagine self-denial as a dramatic moment like martyrdom. But for most believers the cross is mostly a series of small, unseen nails: letting your spouse finish speaking first, giving the credit to a colleague, holding back that cutting reply, answering your child gently when you’re exhausted. Jesus said to take it up “daily.”

Paul says we are “always carrying in the body the putting to death of the Lord Jesus.” The word “always” shows that this is an ongoing way of life. Each time we deny ourselves for the Lord is a small death, and each death lets “the life of Jesus” be revealed. That is why he says, “we don’t faint”: though our outward person is decaying, our inward person is renewed day by day. Self-denial does not make us shrivel; it makes us newer.

Carrying the cross daily needs a rhythm, like eating and sleeping every day. In the morning, give the day to the Lord; during the day, choose to give way in small things; in the evening, review where you carried the cross and where you put it down. Review, Correction, Repetition: this is exactly how, in the eight steps for changing our mindset, a new mindset becomes a new habit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Letting Jesus reign is not a one-off decision but a choice made every morning. Carrying the death of Jesus every day reveals the life of Jesus every day: the self-ruled life of the old self steps down bit by bit, and the self-emptied life of the new self is renewed day by day.
q: Who is God? — God reveals “the life of Jesus” in mortal flesh. What does that tell you about his power?
Who am I? — Are you more drawn to one dramatic act of devotion, or willing to deny yourself daily in small things?
How shall I respond? — On which “small nail” will you take up your cross today?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ cross was not only at Golgotha. For thirty years in Nazareth he submitted to his parents; in Galilee he was so busy with the crowds he had no time to eat; misunderstood by his disciples, he still taught them patiently. The cross at Golgotha was the final summit of a life of daily self-denial.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I am willing to take up my cross daily and follow you, not only in big things but in every small act of giving way, keeping silent and serving today. Let me carry your death in my body and reveal your life, so that my inward person is renewed day by day and the glory goes to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Pray in the morning: “Lord, today I want to deny myself in small things.”
At least once today, let someone finish speaking before you respond
Before bed, write: Which cross did I carry today? Where have I not yet?
lessons.noon: “our inward person is renewed day by day” — Lord, right now I deny myself for you in small things.

lessons.title: Losing Our Life for the Lord
lessons.theme: What we lose for the Lord is what we truly gain

v: For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake will save it.
For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses or forfeits his own self?
For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.

lessons.still: Write on a piece of paper: “For me, to live is ______.” Pause, and honestly fill in the true answer of your heart: success? family? security? Then ask the Lord to help you one day to fill it in, sincerely, with “Christ.”
teach: A mountaineer who clings to everything in his backpack may be dragged down and die in a blizzard; only by dropping the excess weight can he make it down alive. Jesus spoke a truth that sounds like a contradiction: “whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake, the same will save it.”

Then Jesus set a sum: what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose himself? This is the accounting of the kingdom. Earth’s ledger counts how much we own; heaven’s ledger counts whom we live for. From prison Paul wrote, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” When Christ is everything in life, both living and dying are pure gain, with no loss.

“For my sake” is the key phrase in this passage. Losing our life is not for an ideal or to look spiritual, but for Jesus. This is also the difference between the self-emptied life and asceticism: self-emptying is not destroying the self but giving the self to a greater love. Whatever we lose for him, he will keep for ever.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Shift your perspective from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. The self-ruled person tries to save himself and ends up losing; the self-emptied person loses for the Lord and ends up saved. When Jesus receives all the glory, I receive him himself: the best exchange there is.
q: Who is God? — “Whoever will lose his life for my sake, the same will save it.” What does that tell you about Jesus’ promise?
Who am I? — What is the honest answer to your “For me, to live is ______”?
How shall I respond? — What are you holding tightly that you will “lose” for the Lord?
lessons.jesus: In the wilderness Satan showed Jesus the splendour of all the kingdoms of the world and said it would all be his if he would only bow down and worship him. Jesus refused the shortcut of “gaining the whole world” and chose the cross. He lost his life, but the Father raised him from the dead and gave him the name above all things.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, I confess I often try to save my own life, clutching at success, security and other people’s approval. Today I want to lose my life for you, because you are more precious than the whole world. Help me to say: for me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. All glory be to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write “For me, to live is ______,” fill it in honestly and bring it to prayer
Let go of one arrangement in which you sacrifice your spiritual life to “gain the world”
Pray for a missionary or co-worker who is paying a price for the Lord
lessons.noon: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” — Lord, right now you are my life.

lessons.title: The Joy of Self-Denial
lessons.theme: The way of the cross leads to the deepest joy

v: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.

But these things don’t count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to fully testify to the Good News of the grace of God.

lessons.still: Quietly recall the joy that welled up in your heart after a time you denied yourself for the Lord or for someone else. Feel that joy again and say to the Lord, “Lord, thank you that on the road of self-denial there is your joy.”
teach: A farmer is ploughing his field when the plough strikes a chest. He opens it and finds it full of gold, silver and jewels. At once he buries the chest again, goes home, and sells his house, his cattle and everything he owns to buy that field. Onlookers see him giving up everything and think he has lost his mind; but he goes and sells it all “in his joy.” The secret of self-denial is this: you have seen a greater treasure.

The key phrase in Jesus’ parable is “in his joy.” Paul was the same: he knew chains and afflictions lay ahead, yet he said, “nor do I hold my own life dear to myself,” so long as he could “finish my course.” This is not grim endurance but joy drawn by the preciousness of the gospel. When self-denial has no joy, it is often because we have not yet seen clearly the worth of the treasure.

This week we have seen that the cross is willing self-denial, a grain of wheat falling into the ground, a daily choice, a loss for the Lord that is really gain, and finally joy. Next week is the retreat week for the second stage. We will look back over these months of putting down roots and, carrying the joy of self-denial, prepare to enter the season of bearing fruit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When Jesus receives all the glory, I receive the deepest joy. The self-ruled person clutches at everything and grows emptier the tighter he holds; the self-emptied person sells everything in joy. Self-denial is not loss; it is giving all we have in exchange for the priceless treasure, Jesus himself.
q: Who is God? — The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure. What does that show you about how precious God’s kingdom is?
Who am I? — Is your self-denial more like grim endurance, or like going “in his joy” to sell everything?
How shall I respond? — What will you joyfully “sell” for the Lord today?
lessons.jesus: Hebrews says that Jesus, “for the joy that was set before him, endured the cross, despising its shame.” He did not carry the cross with a gloomy face; he saw the joy ahead: our salvation, and being with him in glory. Jesus is both the source and the model of the joy of self-denial.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the treasure hidden in the field. Open my eyes to see that you are more precious than everything, so that denying myself is no longer grim endurance but gladness. I do not hold my life dear; I want only to finish the course you have given me and testify to the gospel of God’s grace, so that you receive the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down one thing you could joyfully let go of for the Lord
Today, with a smile, carry out one act of service you were reluctant to do
Look back over this week’s five lessons and write one sentence about the joy self-denial has brought you
lessons.noon: “In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has” — Lord, right now you are my greatest treasure.

mem.t: Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

lessons.title: Looking Back on the Self-Emptied Life
lessons.theme: This season, the Lord has driven my roots down deep

v: As therefore you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him,
rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, even as you were taught, abounding in it in thanksgiving.
that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love,

lessons.still: Find a quiet place and open up your notes or prayer journal from these twelve weeks. Don’t rush to leaf through them yet. Simply say to the Lord, “Lord, thank you for walking with me this season. Let me see the work you have done in me.”
teach: The months when a tree shows little change above ground are often the very months when its roots are pushing hard through the soil below. Stage Two, Growing: Deeply Rooted, has been a season like that. Others may not see much change in you, but in hidden places the Lord has been driving your roots deeper into Christ.

Look back over these twelve weeks. We affirmed our identity in Christ, studied Philippians, learned confession and forgiveness and being filled with the Spirit; we faced pride, overcame temptation, and learned to be stewards of our time. Then we went deep into the self-emptied life: no longer I. We let God’s word dwell in our hearts, learned to intercede, to discern the Spirit’s guidance, and finally to take up the cross. The thread running through the whole road is the move from the self-ruled life to the self-emptied life.

Paul says, “rooted and built up in him,” and the result is “abounding … in thanksgiving.” The purpose of looking back is not to grade ourselves but to count God’s grace. Today, slowly look through your record of this season, pick out the three clearest things God has done in you, and give thanks for them.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life is not a single insight but a rooting that goes on season after season. A changed mindset brings a changed life, and a changed life brings a changed lifestyle. As we look back, the focus is not on how well I have done but on how Jesus has been reigning in me, and all the glory goes to him.
q: Who is God? — Looking back over these twelve weeks, how have you seen God patiently cultivating you?
Who am I? — In what area have your “roots” gone deepest this season?
How shall I respond? — For which three graces will you give special thanks?
lessons.jesus: Before his public ministry, Jesus spent thirty ordinary years in Nazareth, where before the Father he “increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.” His roots went deep into the Father first, and only then did he bear abundant fruit in three years.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for driving my roots down into you this season. Many times I could not see any growth, yet you were at work all along. I give thanks for your faithfulness. Keep me rooted and built up in you, established in the faith, and overflowing more and more with thankfulness. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Look through your notes from Weeks 14–25 and circle the three deepest things you received
Write the Lord a short thank-you letter listing the graces of this season
Choose the memory verse from this season that touched you most, and recite it once more
lessons.noon: “Rooted and built up in him and established in the faith” — Lord, right now thank you for rooting me in you.

lessons.title: A Humble Testimony
lessons.theme: Counting God’s grace is setting up a stone to mark his works

v: Then Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen, and called its name Ebenezer, saying, “The LORD helped us until now.”
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

lessons.still: Place a small stone or a card in front of you. Quietly recall a moment this season when you chose humility and set yourself aside. Write it on the card, then say, “Until now, the Lord has helped me.”
teach: Along mountain trails you often find little piles of stones, markers left by those who went before, telling later walkers: this path goes through. After Israel’s victory at Mizpah, Samuel set up a stone and named it “Ebenezer,” meaning “Yahweh helped us until now.” A testimony is a stone like that: not a monument to our own achievements but a marker of God’s help.

A humble testimony has one distinguishing mark: the main character is not me but God. Samuel didn’t say, “Until now we have worked very hard,” but, “Yahweh helped us.” James says, “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.” Lifting up is the Lord’s work; humbling ourselves is our part. So a true testimony leaves people praising God, not envying me.

This season you may have experienced giving up an argument, apologising first, praying for someone who hurt you, denying yourself in small things. These were all moments when humility drew out humility. Today, write them down to become your Ebenezer. When you have the chance this weekend, share them humbly with your spiritual companion, so that God receives the glory.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is the key to revival. Humility is laying down power and returning to our place: let people be people and let God be God. A humble testimony turns the focus from me to Jesus and lets him receive all the glory; humility draws out humility, including in those who hear the testimony.
q: Who is God? — “Yahweh helped us until now.” Where have you experienced these words?
Who am I? — In what matter this season did you truly “humble yourself in the sight of the Lord”?
How shall I respond? — Which testimony will you humbly share, and with whom?
lessons.jesus: Jesus healed many people and often told them not to spread it around. But to the man freed from demons he said, “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you, and how he had mercy on you.” The heart of a testimony is the great things the Lord has done.
lessons.pray: Lord, until now you have helped me. Every act of humility and every victory I have experienced this season is your grace, not my achievement. Make my testimony an Ebenezer, so that those who hear it see not me but you, and give the glory to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down two “Ebenezer” testimonies from this season
Humbly share one of those testimonies with a spiritual companion
In your testimony, cut one sentence that boasts about yourself and add one more that thanks the Lord
lessons.noon: “The LORD helped us until now.” — Lord, right now I give thanks for your help all along the way.

lessons.title: Forgetting What Is Behind, Reaching for What Is Ahead
lessons.theme: Not bound by the past, pressing on toward the goal

v: Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect; but I press on, that I may take hold of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus.
Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
“Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old.
Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.

lessons.still: Gently sweep both hands behind you, as if setting down the burdens at your back; then stretch both hands forward, like a runner reaching for the finish line. Quietly say, “Lord, I forget what is behind and reach for what is ahead.”
teach: A runner who keeps looking back not only slows down but may stumble. When Paul says “forgetting the things which are behind,” he does not mean amnesia, but refusing to let the past set today’s direction. Two things behind us can drag us back: the guilt of failure, which makes us afraid to run again, and the pride of success, which makes us think we have already arrived.

In verse 12 Paul first says, “Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect.” This mature apostle was still pressing on. His drive did not come from his own resolve but from the fact that he had been “taken hold of by Christ Jesus.” The Lord took hold of me first, so I press on to take hold of him. Isaiah, too, says, “Behold, I will do a new thing.” God is the God who makes rivers in the desert.

In Week 15 we studied Philippians and learned about forgetting what is behind and reaching for what is ahead. Reading it again now, during retreat, is about handing this half-year’s weaknesses to the cross and handing its progress to the Lord, rather than resting on our laurels. The goal is still ahead: to be more like Jesus, and to let him reign more and more.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility overcomes pride. Not thinking we have already arrived is returning to our place. Failure does not condemn me and success does not bind me, because my focus is on Jesus, not on myself. Pressing on toward the goal means moving towards this aim: letting Jesus reign and giving the glory to him.
q: Who is God? — He is the God who says, “I will do a new thing.” What hope does that give you for the next stage?
Who am I? — What is dragging you back: the guilt of failure, or the pride of success?
How shall I respond? — What from your past will you hand to the Lord today and not look back on?
lessons.jesus: After his resurrection, beside the lake, Jesus asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?” He did not drag up the past; he healed the wound of Peter’s three denials and then said, “Feed my sheep.” Jesus helped Peter forget what was behind, reach for what was ahead, and start running again.
lessons.pray: Lord, I hand to you the failures and guilt of this half-year, and I give back to you all its progress and credit. I don’t think I have already arrived; I want to press on to take hold of that for which you took hold of me. Do a new thing in my life, and let me press on toward the goal. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down one thing from the past to “forget,” pray over it, then tear it up
Write down one goal you will “reach for” in the next stage
Memorise this week’s verse: Philippians 3:13–14
lessons.noon: “Forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before” — Lord, right now I let go of what is behind and run toward you.

lessons.title: Stage Self-Review
lessons.theme: Examining ourselves honestly in the Lord’s light, to prepare for the next step

v: Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.
See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.
Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD.

lessons.still: Quietly read Psalm 139:23–24 twice, the second time more slowly. Then say to the Lord, “Lord, I am transparent before you. Shine your light, not to condemn me, but to lead me.”
teach: A regular health check is not meant to frighten us but to catch problems early so we can go on living healthily. Our spiritual life needs a check-up too. The self-review in retreat week is like a full examination before the Lord: not comparing ourselves with others, nor with our ideal selves, but honestly seeing who we are right now.

David’s prayer is remarkable. He does not examine himself and then report to God; he asks God to “search” and “try” him, to see “if there is any wicked way in me,” and then asks God to “lead me in the everlasting way.” The goal of self-review is direction, not a score. Lamentations, too, says that we search our ways in order to “turn again to Yahweh.”

With a prayerful heart, complete this stage’s spiritual health self-review and compare it with your results from Stage One. Notice where you have grown and where you have stalled. Give thanks for the growth, hand the stalled areas to the Lord, and write down one or two directions to practise especially in the next stage. Honesty is where blessing begins, and grace is always bigger than our scores.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Review and Correction, from the eight steps for changing our mindset, happen right here. Reviewing ourselves before the Lord is humility, admitting we have not yet arrived, and it is also faith, trusting that the Lord will lead the way ahead. The focus is not on a score but on letting Jesus reign more fully in the next stage.
q: Who is God? — God searches us in order to “lead me in the everlasting way.” How does that shape the way you approach this self-review?
Who am I? — Compared with Stage One, where is your clearest growth, and where have you most clearly stalled?
How shall I respond? — What are the one or two directions you most need to practise in the next stage?
lessons.jesus: Jesus told the Samaritan woman the truth about her life, yet he did not shame her; instead he revealed to her that he was the Messiah. She ran back to her town and said, “Come, see a man who told me everything that I did.” Being seen through by Jesus brought her freedom and a mission.
lessons.pray: God, search me and know my heart; see if there is any wicked way in me. I am not afraid to be seen through by you, because you see me fully and love me deeply. Lead me through this self-review: let me give thanks for growth, hand my weaknesses to you, and walk in the everlasting way. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.

Compare with your Stage One results and write down one area of growth and one area where you have stalled
Write down one or two directions to practise especially in the next stage
lessons.noon: “Search me, God, and know my heart.” — Lord, right now I open myself before you; please lead me.

lessons.title: Resolving to Bear Fruit
lessons.theme: After deep roots comes the fruit of the Spirit

v: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
“In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.

lessons.still: Quietly bring to mind the people closest to you: family, colleagues, brothers and sisters. Bring their names before the Lord one by one, saying, “Lord, between me and them, let your fruit grow.”
teach: During the years a fruit tree is putting down roots, the farmer waits patiently; once the roots are deep, fruit begins to appear on the branches. Stage One was Rooting, Stage Two was Growing deep roots, and Stage Three takes us into Fruiting. But remember: fruit is not a decoration stuck on from outside; it grows out of life itself. The deeper the roots, the sweeter the fruit.

Paul speaks of “the fruit of the Spirit”: fruit in the singular, with nine flavours: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. It is not nine separate tests but the whole life of Christ flowing out. Jesus said, “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit.” The purpose of bearing fruit is the Father’s glory.

Most of this fruit grows within relationships. Without people there is no one to be patient with; without conflict, gentleness never shows. In the next stage we will learn “920”: every person in my life is my “2”; I practise the “0” of the self-emptied life; and the “9” is the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Today, resolve to carry the roots of these months into the season of bearing fruit.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 920: every person in my life is my “2”; I practise the “0” of the self-emptied life; the “9” is the ninefold fruit of the Spirit. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. A deeply rooted life must bear fruit in relationships, build God’s kingdom system, and bring the Father glory.
q: Who is God? — “In this my Father is glorified.” What does that show you about how much God delights in his children bearing fruit?
Who am I? — Of the nine flavours of the fruit, which is most lacking in your relationships?
How shall I respond? — What resolution will you make as you enter the next stage of bearing fruit?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the perfect display of the fruit of the Spirit: his love reached even his enemies, his joy was not taken from him even before the cross, his patience bore with slow-hearted disciples, his gentleness would not break a bruised reed. He said, “I am the vine. You are the branches.” All our fruit comes from him.
lessons.pray: Heavenly Father, thank you for leading me through these deeply rooted months. I resolve to enter the season of bearing fruit. Holy Spirit, in every relationship of mine produce love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control, so that the Father is glorified and your kingdom system is built. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down the names of the five most important “2”s in your life
Choose the fruit of the Spirit you most lack and make it your prayer for the next stage
Write a prayer of resolution, share it with your spiritual companion and ask them to pray for you
lessons.noon: “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit” — Lord, right now let your fruit grow in my relationships.
